item.title: An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems [1] (CHI 2026), Anna Martin-Boyle and Harmanpreet Kaur (University of Minnesota), with William Humphreys, Martha Brown, and Cara Leckey at NASA Langley Research Center, build a schema of how working scientists actually judge LLM answers about their own field, arguing that automated metrics miss how they assess those answers.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming scholarly tasks like search and summarization, but their reliability remains uncertain. Current evaluation metrics for testing LLM reliability are primarily automated approaches that prioritize efficiency and scalability, but lack contextual nuance and fail to reflect how scientific domain experts assess LLM outputs in practice. We developed and validated a schema for evaluating LLM errors in scholarly question-answering systems that reflects the assessment strategies of practicing scientists. In collaboration with domain experts, we identified 20 error patterns across seven categories through thematic analysis of 68 question-answer pairs. We validated this schema through contextual inquiries with 10 additional scientists, which showed not only which errors experts naturally identify but also how structured evaluation schemas can help them detect previously overlooked issues. Domain experts use systematic assessment strategies, including technical precision testing, value-based evaluation, and meta-evaluation of their own practices. We discuss implications for supporting expert evaluation of LLM outputs, including opportunities for personalized, schema-driven tools that adapt to individual evaluation patterns and expertise levels.

Methods

The study runs a retrieval-augmented QA system over scientific papers (documents are chunked, vectorized, retrieved per question, and fed to an LLM that generates a long-form answer), then examines how domain experts evaluate its output in two phases. The LLM-generated answers are the object of evaluation throughout, and the two phases use different sets of them: the Phase 1 answers became the coded data that built the schema, while in Phase 2 a fresh batch was the material experts evaluated to validate it.

  • Phase 1, schema development. Three NASA Langley scientists took part. Two posed questions about papers they had authored (28 in aeroacoustics, 40 in non-destructive evaluation) and the QA system generated an LLM answer to each, so the ground truth was known to the evaluator. The third wrote no questions and was kept aside to label those answers for errors independently, a perspective the authors kept unbiased by not having that expert author any of the questions. Thematic analysis of the resulting 68 question-answer pairs yielded 20 recurring error patterns, organized into seven categories. The complete schema is in The Schema below.
  • Phase 2, schema validation. Ten additional scientists each wrote questions about their own papers, and the system generated LLM answers that the experts evaluated in think-aloud contextual inquiries. They evaluated unaided first, then with the schema (the Phase 1 list of 20 error patterns grouped into seven categories) in hand, to test whether it helped them catch errors they had missed.

Across both phases the authors collected 188 expert-posed questions and sorted them into 11 question types (a separate classification from the error schema, grouping the questions rather than the errors):

  • Methodological Inquiry and Improvement: compares approaches and asks how methods could be transferred or refined.
  • Meta-Analysis and Contextualization: asks about institutional motivations and synthesizes insights across multiple papers.
  • Critical Evaluation and Validation: probes assumptions and biases, and whether research choices were adequately justified.
  • Application and Practical Implications: asks how findings translate to real-world use and what tradeoffs implementation brings.
  • Technical Details and Specifications: asks for the parameters, equations, or configurations needed to replicate the work.
  • Definitions and Concepts: asks to clarify core ideas and key terms.
  • Future Directions and Extrapolation: looks past current findings to next steps and where the research is heading.
  • Binary / Factual Verification: asks to confirm or deny a discrete fact, without interpretation.
  • External Context: asks for knowledge beyond the paper, such as external standards or developments since publication.
  • Numerical Analysis and Derivation: asks the system to calculate or reason mathematically with data from the paper.
  • Procedural Information: asks how a study was conducted, focusing on the sequence of steps.

They then mapped the error patterns against each question type (Figure 2, the cover heatmap).

The Schema

The full taxonomy, for reference: 20 error patterns under seven categories, paraphrased from the paper’s Tables 1 and 2 [1]. Hallucinations are a single pattern broken out into seven sub-types.

  • Incorrect answer
    • Completely incorrect: the answer is entirely wrong.
    • Partially incorrect: a mix of right and wrong, covering basic accuracy slips, misinterpreting paper content, self-contradiction, reference confusion, and misread tables or equations.
    • Superfluous content: irrelevant or unnecessary information.
  • Hallucinations (plausible-looking content that is fabricated or false)
    • Terminology: invented or wrongly defined terms and acronyms.
    • Numerical data: made-up statistics, measurements, or metrics.
    • Mathematical constructs: invented equations, formulae, or relationships.
    • Technical content: false technical characteristics, properties, limitations, or capabilities.
    • External context and world knowledge: wrong general science or related-literature claims.
    • Document structure: invented page, section, table, or figure numbers.
    • Citation information: fabricated citations or parts of them (authors, dates, titles, venues, DOIs, page numbers).
  • Incomplete answer
    • Major omissions: important content left out: an ignored section, a missed main point, an ignored paper in a multi-document question, an incomplete definition, missing references, or chronological gaps.
    • Lacking details: high-level concepts present but lower-level detail missing.
    • Multimedia comprehension: fails to connect formats, for example not linking a table to its caption or in-text reference.
  • Question interpretation
    • Question misinterpretation: a wrong reading that leads to a wrong answer.
    • Question redirection: answers a different question than the one asked.
  • Synthesis issues
    • Document linking failure: can’t tie information to the right document across multiple papers.
    • Chronological confusion: misreads temporal relationships.
    • Disjointed response: fragmented or poorly integrated, for example discussing each paper in isolation.
    • Source confusion: misattributes information across papers.
  • Formatting issues
    • Verbosity: unnecessarily wordy or repetitive.
    • Notation errors: incorrect technical notation.
    • Language issues: improper wording, spelling, grammar, or syntax.
    • Inconsistent referencing: inconsistent in how it references content.
  • System failures
    • LLM limitations: model-inherent issues such as limited context length, no multi-modal understanding, and no access to external libraries.
    • Retrieval failures: the retriever did not supply the needed context.
    • Data structure issues: internal data-organization problems leaking into outputs.

Results

Because this is a qualitative HCI study rather than a leaderboard, the results are the schema itself and the evaluation behavior it exposes, validated through the two-phase design (3 experts in development, 10 in validation, all recruited through NASA Langley’s internal networks).

  • The schema generalizes to a second expert group. All seven categories reappeared in Phase 2’s independent coding of the 10 new experts’ unprompted feedback, which suggests expert error-spotting is consistent across people rather than an artifact of the development team.
  • Experts evaluate with structured strategies, not gut reaction. They apply technical precision testing, value-based assessment tied to research use, and meta-evaluation of their own checking process, behavior that automated metrics do not model.
  • The schema is also a scaffold. Giving experts the schema during contextual inquiries turned up errors they had overlooked when evaluating unaided. The most common were hallucinated or misattributed citations, but experts also caught missing tables and figures, chronological gaps, disjointed responses, and missed main points once the inventory prompted them to look. The taxonomy does double duty as a checklist for human review.
  • Error profiles differ by question type (Figure 2). The 11 question types do not fail the same way, which suggests evaluation and mitigation should be differentiated by question type rather than applied uniformly.

My Notes

  • This is the human-process complement to the automated-benchmark line, and it is openly skeptical of it. Benchmarks like ExpertQA [2] and ResearchQA [3] push toward scalable automated scoring, while this paper argues those metrics are too coarse to capture how experts judge, and studies the assessment process itself. The two programs answer different questions, what a good answer should contain versus how a scientist decides whether it does, and the schema is the missing description of the second.

  • Evaluators grading answers about their own papers provides strong but narrow ground truth. Recruiting scientists to assess QA output on work they authored removes the usual annotator-knowledge gap, since they know what the correct answer is. The cost is scale and breadth: 3 experts in development and 10 in validation, all from one research center, which makes the schema’s categories credible but their relative frequencies hard to generalize.

  • The schema-as-scaffold result is the practically useful finding. That structured prompts help experts catch overlooked errors matches a long line of checklist research in medicine and aviation, where externalizing tacit criteria improves detection. It points at the paper’s own proposed direction: schema-driven review tools.

  • Error-by-question-type echoes the cross-benchmark pattern that difficulty is not uniform. ExpertQA found list, advice, and opinion questions hardest [2], and this paper independently finds error profiles vary by question type. The convergence across an automated benchmark and a qualitative study is the stronger signal: question type, not just domain, is a primary driver of LLM-QA difficulty.

References

  1. Martin-Boyle, A., Humphreys, W., Brown, M., Leckey, C., Kaur, H.. “An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems.” CHI 2026 (arXiv:2602.21059), February 24, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21059
  2. Malaviya, C., Lee, S., Chen, S., Sieber, E., Yatskar, M., Roth, D.. “ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers.” NAACL 2024 (arXiv:2309.07852), September 14, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07852
  3. Li S. Yifei, Allen Chang, Malaviya, C., Yatskar, M.. “ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2509.00496), August 30, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00496

Related Posts

  • ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers: the automated benchmark this study implicitly critiques, and the source of the matching question-type-difficulty finding.
  • TruthfulQA: Are Larger LLMs More Truthful?: an early factuality benchmark whose single-metric framing this paper argues is too coarse for how experts actually judge answers.
  • AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 Queries: another domain (law) where expert-grounded error analysis exposes failures automated scoring understates.

item.title: Temperature’s Effect on My Running Efficiency
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

I finally got data to back it up on temperature’s effect to my running efficiency:

  • Yesterday 89F: 6.22mi pace 10’15”/mi w/ avg HR 133bpm
  • Today 61F: 6.05mi pace 9’13”/mi w/ avg HR 133bpm (same)

So 28F increase cost 1’02”/mi pace w/ HR constant! Both routes are equally flat (East Sammamish Lake Trail vs Elliott Bay Trail).

For today’s run I even did 4x20s strides clocking max 5’26”/mi!

Photos were yesterday’s run and today in office.

Originally posted on Mastodon.

item.title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Automated Design of Agentic Systems [1] (ICLR 2025), Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, and Jeff Clune at the University of British Columbia and the Vector Institute argue that the design of LLM-powered agents should itself be automated, and introduce Meta Agent Search as a first instance.

Researchers are investing substantial effort in developing powerful general-purpose agents, wherein Foundation Models are used as modules within agentic systems (e.g. Chain-of-Thought, Self-Reflection, Toolformer). However, the history of machine learning teaches us that hand-designed solutions are eventually replaced by learned solutions. We describe a newly forming research area, Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS), which aims to automatically create powerful agentic system designs, including inventing novel building blocks and/or combining them in new ways. We further demonstrate that there is an unexplored yet promising approach within ADAS where agents can be defined in code and new agents can be automatically discovered by a meta agent programming ever better ones in code. Given that most programming languages are Turing Complete, this approach theoretically enables the learning of any possible agentic system: including novel prompts, tool use, workflows, and combinations thereof. We present a simple yet effective algorithm named Meta Agent Search to demonstrate this idea, where a meta agent iteratively programs interesting new agents based on an ever-growing archive of previous discoveries. Through extensive experiments across multiple domains including coding, science, and math, we show that our algorithm can progressively invent agents with novel designs that greatly outperform state-of-the-art hand-designed agents. Importantly, we consistently observe the surprising result that agents invented by Meta Agent Search maintain superior performance even when transferred across domains and models, demonstrating their robustness and generality. Provided we develop it safely, our work illustrates the potential of an exciting new research direction toward automatically designing ever-more powerful agentic systems to benefit humanity.

Methods

The authors cast Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS) as an optimization problem with three components (Figure 2):

  • Search space: the set of agent designs the method can represent. Meta Agent Search makes this Python code: an agent is a forward(task) function that may call foundation-model APIs, use tools, keep internal state, and compose sub-agents. Because the language is Turing-complete, the space in principle covers any prompt, tool-use pattern, or workflow, not just variations on a fixed template.
  • Search algorithm: how the space is explored. A meta agent (a frontier LLM, GPT-4 in the experiments) reads an archive of previously discovered agents and programs a new one.
  • Evaluation function: how a candidate is scored. Each new agent runs on a held-out validation split of the target task, and its accuracy or F1 is the signal the meta agent maximizes.

The search loop is short. The meta agent works against a roughly 100-line framework that supplies basic primitives like foundation-model queries and prompt formatting, so it only writes the forward function, the same trick FunSearch [2] used to evolve programs from a small set of given building blocks. Each iteration runs four steps:

  • The archive is optionally seeded with baseline agents such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Refine.
  • Conditioned on the whole archive, the meta agent writes a high-level description of a new agent (the prompt asks for one that is “interestingly new”) and then its code, with two self-reflection passes meant to keep the design novel.
  • The candidate runs on validation data. If it errors, the meta agent revises the code, repeating up to five times.
  • The working agent and its score are appended to the archive, and the next iteration conditions on the larger archive.

The archive is the memory that lets each iteration build on the last. Because it stores each agent’s full source code, not just a description, a new agent can copy and recombine code from earlier ones rather than start from scratch. The paper shows several designs discovered on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) reusing earlier “stepping stones”: a multi-chain-of-thought-then-ensemble pattern that first appeared at iteration 3, and expert-critic ideas from iterations 5, 11, and 12 that the best agent later combined.

Results

The experiments span three settings, all run with the same algorithm and only task-specific prompt text changed. The ARC abstraction benchmark is the case study. Four benchmarks covering reading, math, science, and multi-task reasoning (DROP, MGSM, MMLU, GPQA) are the main comparison. Held-out tasks and swapped base models test transfer. In every setting the meta agent is GPT-4, while the discovered agents and all baselines are scored with the cheaper GPT-3.5 over five runs each, reporting median accuracy or F1 with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval. The baselines are the standard hand-designed scaffolds (Chain-of-Thought, self-consistency, Self-Refine, LLM-Debate, Quality-Diversity, Step-back Abstraction, Role Assignment) plus the prompt-optimization method OPRO [3] , so the comparison isolates what searching over code buys beyond searching over prompts.

The ARC case study shows the search dynamic most clearly. Over 25 iterations, held-out test accuracy climbs from about 6% to 14%, above every hand-designed baseline. The left panel of Figure 3 tracks that climb and marks the iterations where key ideas first appeared. The right panel shows the best agent found, a “Structured Feedback and Ensemble” design that generates five chains of thought, routes them through three expert critics (efficiency, readability, simplicity) plus a human-like critic, and ensembles three refinement passes.

Across the four reasoning benchmarks the same ranking holds, and the margins are largest exactly where the base model already has the knowledge but makes avoidable errors:

  • Reading comprehension (DROP): 79.4 F1 against 65.8 for the best hand-designed agent, a 13.6-point gain.
  • Math (MGSM): 53.4% against 39.0% for LLM-Debate, the best baseline, a 14.4-point gain.
  • Multi-task (MMLU) and science (GPQA): smaller margins (69.6% vs. 67.6%, 34.6% vs. 32.9%), which the authors attribute to the base model lacking the underlying knowledge rather than the scaffold failing.
  • Cross-domain transfer: the top-3 agents found on MGSM, moved to held-out GSM8K and GSM-Hard, add 25.9% and 13.2% over the baselines. Moved to non-math MMLU and DROP they still beat the hand-designed scaffolds.
  • Cross-model transfer: the top-3 ARC agents found with GPT-3.5 keep their lead when run on Claude Haiku, GPT-4, and Claude Sonnet, with Sonnet reaching nearly 50% on ARC.

Meta Agent Search wins every column of the head-to-head, and it beats OPRO in all four domains, the result the authors lean on to argue that searching over whole agents, not just prompts, is what pays off.

My Notes

  • Transfer is the result that matters, and it comes from the scaffolds being domain-agnostic: it outweighs the ARC gain, a large relative jump on small absolute numbers (human-level is around 80% [4]). Scaffolds discovered on one task keep working on different tasks and on different base models, because the designs are reasoning-and-control patterns that manipulate model calls without encoding the task itself, with the task-specific content kept in the prompt the agent receives rather than in its code, so they behave less like solvers tuned to one benchmark. This parallels Promptbreeder [5], where evolved prompts transferred, but here the unit that transfers is executable code, a broader portability claim. The search optimized accuracy on a single domain with no cross-domain objective, yet the agents transfer anyway, which is good held-out evidence that the generality is real rather than fit to one benchmark. Optimizing for it directly is still untried.
  • Code as the search space: earlier automated-prompting work (OPRO [3], APE [6], Promptbreeder) searches over strings fed to a fixed scaffold, and DSPy [7] compiles a human-written module graph, optimizing the prompts and demonstrations inside it rather than the graph itself. ADAS widens the space to code, so the meta agent can invent new control flow (loops, early-exit, ensembles, self-critique), not just better prompts inside an existing shape. AFlow [8] , published around the same time, makes a different trade: it searches a graph over a fixed library of operators with Monte Carlo tree search. ADAS and AFlow leave open whether to search over open-ended code or a fixed operator graph.
  • The archive both enables the search and makes it expensive: Meta Agent Search is a novelty-seeking search with an LLM as the mutation operator, and the archive of past designs lets each round build on earlier ones. That same archive makes each step expensive: 25 iterations on ARC and 30 on the reasoning benchmarks, each generating one candidate, running two self-reflection passes, and allowing up to five error-driven refinements, with every accepted candidate scored on the full validation set. Scaling to harder benchmarks runs into the sample-efficiency limit that prompt-optimization methods like OPRO [3] also hit, and surrogate scoring to avoid running every candidate on the full eval set is the obvious follow-up.
  • On the intrinsic-to-extrinsic spectrum of self-improving agents: that spectrum [9], from Liu and van der Schaar, runs from agents that set their own learning loop (intrinsic) to loops fully fixed by humans (extrinsic). ADAS is more intrinsic than the earlier prompt-search optimizers: the meta agent reasons over the archive in an open-ended code space to decide what to build next, which is autonomous metacognitive planning rather than algorithmic mutation, and code can in principle express agents that improve themselves. But the parts that decide what counts as better stay human-fixed: the objective (validation accuracy on a chosen benchmark), the evaluation function, the archive mechanism, the stopping point. So it is a mixed case, not the fully extrinsic end: autonomous proposal inside a human-designed objective and loop. The paper’s own thesis, that hand-designed solutions are eventually replaced by learned ones, applies to the agents but not yet to the loop that finds them. Making that loop learned, a self-referential meta agent that improves itself, is the direction the authors flag as future work. The same team took that step in the Darwin Gödel Machine [10] , where agents rewrite their own code against a growing archive of variants.
  • The “provided we develop it safely” caveat points at a real property of the method: the abstract’s closing line is not boilerplate. A loop that proposes and executes arbitrary code is a capability-elicitation concern once it is pointed at an open-ended objective rather than a sandboxed benchmark, closer in shape to AutoGPT-style self-improvement than to prompt search. Clune’s earlier argument for AI-generating algorithms [11] is the right context for reading the paper’s scope.

References

  2. Romera-Paredes, B., Barekatain, M., Novikov, A., Balog, M., Kumar, M. P., Dupont, E., Ruiz, F. J. R., Ellenberg, J.   • Promptbreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement Via Prompt Evolution: evolutionary prompt search whose transfer result ADAS echoes, with executable code rather than a prompt as the unit that transfers.
  • EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers: the same LLM-as-mutation-operator pattern over a narrower, prompt-only search space.

item.title: ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In ResearchQA [1], Li S. Yifei, Allen Chang, Chaitanya Malaviya, and Mark Yatskar (University of Pennsylvania), the team behind ExpertQA [2], scale expert-style scholarly QA evaluation from 32 fields to 75 by mining queries and grading rubrics from survey articles instead of paying domain experts to author them.

Evaluating long-form responses to research queries heavily relies on expert annotators, restricting attention to areas like AI where researchers can conveniently enlist colleagues. Yet, research expertise is abundant: survey articles consolidate knowledge spread across the literature. We introduce ResearchQA, a resource for evaluating LLM systems by distilling survey articles from 75 research fields into 21K queries and 160K rubric items. Queries and rubrics are jointly derived from survey sections, where rubric items list query-specific answer evaluation criteria, i.e., citing papers, making explanations, and describing limitations. 31 Ph.D. annotators in 8 fields judge that 90% of queries reflect Ph.D. information needs and 87% of rubric items warrant emphasis of a sentence or longer. We leverage ResearchQA to evaluate 18 systems in 7.6K head-to-heads. No parametric or retrieval-augmented system we evaluate exceeds 70% on covering rubric items, and the highest-ranking system shows 75% coverage. Error analysis reveals that the highest-ranking system fully addresses less than 11% of citation rubric items, 48% of limitation items, and 49% of comparison items. We release our data to facilitate more comprehensive multi-field evaluations.

Methods

The core idea is that a survey article is pre-distilled expert knowledge: its section structure already encodes what questions a field cares about and what a complete answer must contain. ResearchQA turns that structure into an evaluation set through a four-stage pipeline, with quality filters at each step:

  • Extract top venues per field. Pull each field’s top-20 venues by h5-index from Google Scholar Metrics, then manually redistribute Google Scholar’s 257 fields into 94 cleaner ones (660 venues total), since its categories are alternately too granular and too broad. The final test split spans the 75 fields that yield enough qualifying surveys downstream.
  • Retrieve survey articles. Fetch candidate survey articles from those venues via Crossref, Semantic Scholar, and S2ORC, then filter to genuine literature reviews (134K downloadable articles → 54K surveys).
  • Generate queries from survey sections. Turn each qualifying survey section into a self-contained research query plus a reference answer, filtered for self-containment, low answer variability, and citation content.
  • Generate rubrics. For each query, build a hybrid rubric of up to 8 items naming query-specific criteria a good answer should meet. The rubric is fixed once per query, built from the survey’s own reference answer rather than from any candidate response, and the same rubric then scores every system’s answer to that query. Two rubrics are drafted and merged: a survey rubric conditioned on the query plus the survey’s reference answer, and a parametric rubric conditioned on the query alone. The union is deduplicated, reranked by importance, and stripped of items that cite papers unmatchable on Google Scholar, keeping the top 8 (about 7.5 on average, ~61% from the survey rubric). Each item comes from one of three prompt types, sampled for topic diversity:
    • Information-based items ask for a specific statement, finding, opinion, or comparison.
    • Depth-based items ask for elaboration or explanation.
    • Citation-based items ask whether the answer cites a specific article.

The result is 21K queries and 160K rubric items spanning 75 fields across 7 domains, weighted toward health sciences and medicine. Thirty-one Ph.D. annotators across 8 fields then validate the artifact: they judge that 90% of queries reflect genuine Ph.D. information needs and that 87% of rubric items are worth a sentence or more in a complete answer.

Results

ResearchQA evaluates 18 systems in four classes (parametric LLMs, naive retrieval, production retrieval, and deep-research agents) across 7.6K head-to-head battles. Each answer is scored on two expert-validated metrics: average rubric coverage % (an absolute 0–4 score per rubric item, validated to agree with plurality Ph.D. labels 74% of the time when coverage and direct judgments are ensembled) and an Elo leaderboard score from pairwise preferences. Rubric items map to dimensions sampled from ScholarQABench and SciArena, including correctness, citations, coverage, relevance, organization, and attribution.

The headline is a ceiling, not a ranking:

  • No parametric or retrieval-augmented system clears 70% coverage. The top system overall, Perplexity’s deep-research agent, reaches 75.29%, leaving a quarter of rubric items uncovered even at the frontier.
  • The gap is worst exactly where it matters for scholarship. The highest-ranking system fully addresses fewer than 11% of citation rubric items, 48% of limitation items, and 49% of comparison items: it answers the question but rarely cites the right work, names the caveats, or contrasts alternatives.
  • Naive retrieval barely helps. Bolting a simple retriever onto a parametric model often fails to lift coverage, and on average the same model differs by only 7.6% coverage between naive and production retrieval.
  • The ceiling isn’t a verbosity artifact. Because coverage is recall-based, longer answers mechanically tend to cover more, so the obvious worry is that the metric just rewards length. Figure 6 bounds that: coverage rises with answer length but plateaus around 85% past ~2,000 words (about four pages), even though deep-research systems write up to 3,000 words while human-written answers on similar topics average under 300 words. The ceiling holds at the longest answers, so the uncovered rubric items are genuine omissions, not a side effect of short responses.

My Notes

  • Survey-mining swaps the expensive ingredient in ExpertQA for a scalable one. ExpertQA [2] paid 484 experts to author 2,177 questions in 32 fields, and that human-authoring step is exactly what capped its size and breadth. ResearchQA, from the same group, treats published surveys as compiled expertise and mines 21K queries across 75 fields from them, a roughly 10× scale-up that trades direct expert authoring for the assumption that survey sections already encode what experts would ask. The 90% Ph.D.-endorsement rate is the evidence that the proxy mostly holds.

  • The evaluation target moved from per-claim attribution to rubric coverage, which measures a different failure. ExpertQA asked whether each emitted claim was supported by its cited evidence (a precision-style check on what the model said). ResearchQA’s rubric coverage asks whether the answer contains what a good answer should (a recall-style check on what the model omitted). The two are complementary, and ResearchQA’s low citation-coverage number (under 11% of citation items fully addressed) shows the recall view exposes a failure the precision view can miss: a system can avoid unsupported claims simply by never attempting the citations a complete answer needs.

  • Rubric coverage inherits the LLM-as-judge grounding problem it is trying to escape. The metric is only as trustworthy as the automatic judge scoring each rubric item, and the paper reports 74% coverage agreement and 69% pairwise agreement with Ph.D. humans, only reached after ensembling. That is squarely the contested LLM-as-judge reliability question, where prior work has shown LLM evaluators can be pushed to misrank answers outright [3].

  • A reusable recipe for any field with a survey literature. The pipeline needs only Google Scholar venue rankings and survey-article databases, so the same machinery could generate domain-specific evaluation sets wherever review articles exist, without recruiting a single expert. The bottleneck for trustworthy domain evaluation then shifts from expert availability to survey availability, which is far less scarce.

References

  1. Li S. Yifei, Allen Chang, Malaviya, C., Yatskar, M.. “ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2509.00496), August 30, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00496
  2. Malaviya, C., Lee, S., Chen, S., Sieber, E., Yatskar, M., Roth, D.. “ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers.” NAACL 2024 (arXiv:2309.07852), September 14, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07852
  3. Wang, P., Li, L., Chen, L., Cai, Z., Zhu, D., Lin, B., Cao, Y., Liu, Q., Liu, T., Sui, Z. “Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators.” ACL 2024 (arXiv:2305.17926), May 29, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17926

Related Posts

  • ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers: the direct predecessor from the same lab, which paid experts to author questions and grade claim-level attribution rather than mining surveys for rubrics.
  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: the constructive side, giving statistical guarantees on which claims to keep where ResearchQA only measures how much a system covers.
  • TruthfulQA: Are Larger LLMs More Truthful?: an earlier factuality benchmark that ResearchQA pushes into long-form, citation-bearing scholarly answers.

item.title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget [1] (ICML 2026), Xi Wang, Anushri Suresh, Alvin Zhang, Rishi More, William Jurayj, Benjamin Van Durme, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Daniel Khashabi, and Eric Nalisnick (Johns Hopkins University and Apple) recast the question of when to stop a reasoning chain as distribution-free risk control, and add a lower threshold that gives up early on problems the model is unlikely to solve.

Reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs) enable test-time scaling, with dataset-level accuracy improving as the token budget increases, motivating adaptive reasoning — spending tokens when they improve reliability and stopping early when additional computation is unlikely to help. However, setting the token budget, as well as the threshold for adaptive reasoning, is a practical challenge that entails a fundamental risk-accuracy trade-off. We re-frame the budget setting problem as risk control, limiting the error rate while minimizing compute. Our framework introduces an upper threshold that stops reasoning when the model is confident (risking incorrect output) and a novel parametric lower threshold that preemptively stops unsolvable instances (risking premature stoppage). Given a target risk and a validation set, we use distribution-free risk control to optimally specify these stopping mechanisms. For scenarios with multiple budget controlling criteria, we incorporate an efficiency loss to select the most computationally efficient exiting mechanism. Empirical results across diverse reasoning tasks and models demonstrate the effectiveness of our risk control approach, demonstrating computational efficiency gains from the lower threshold and ensemble stopping mechanisms while adhering to the user-specified risk target.

Methods

Signals and the two thresholds

Conformal Thinking treats a reasoning chain as a sequence of chunks (the text between consecutive \n\n breaks) and, at the end of each growing chunk, reads a scalar signal off the model — oriented so that a larger means the model looks more confident it has converged. The signal is itself a choice: denotes which signal (a function of the trace so far) and its value at chunk , and the choice of is one more thing to calibrate. The paper compares four:

  • Confidence [2] — force the model to begin its final answer, greedily roll it out, and score that rollout by its length-normalized log-likelihood (higher = more confident).
  • EAT (Entropy After /think) [3] — at that same forced-answer point, read the entropy of the next-token distribution instead of rolling an answer out; low entropy means the model is peaked on what to answer.
  • Trained probe [4] — a probe trained on AIME (a hard math-competition benchmark) to predict convergence (Qwen3-8B only).
  • Token count — the raw number of tokens generated so far, a length-only baseline.

Both thresholds operate on — one on its current value, one on its trajectory — and both are chosen to respect a user-specified error tolerance rather than tuned by hand:

  • Upper threshold : a level on the current value of — stop once clears , on the assumption that the model has converged on its answer. This is the standard confidence-based early-exit rule, and it controls the false positive risk of stopping with a wrong answer.

  • Lower threshold : the paper’s new mechanism, and the reason it is not a fixed floor. is a rising schedule — a logistic (sigmoid) curve in , the tokens spent by chunk , climbing from a low asymptote toward a high one (typically ) as the budget is consumed:

    with slope and its midpoint at a fraction of the budget. The chain gives up at the first chunk where confidence falls to or below the floor, . Because the floor keeps rising, the model must raise its confidence to stay above it; if confidence stalls — the signature of an instance it is unlikely to solve — the floor overtakes it and reasoning halts before the full budget is spent. This is what makes the rule a constraint on the trajectory of rather than its current value, and it controls the false negative risk of giving up on an instance more reasoning would have solved. Of these symbols, is the running token count and the fixed budget; the schedule’s shape — slope , midpoint , and low asymptote — is what risk control calibrates.

The two thresholds save tokens in complementary places: the upper one trims wasted reasoning after the model has effectively converged, while the lower one avoids spending tokens on instances where further reasoning is unlikely to pay off. The next figure plots a confidence trajectory against token usage for Qwen3-8B on AIME. On an unsolvable instance (left), confidence fluctuates and never reaches the upper threshold, so the lower threshold halts the run before it consumes the full budget. On a solvable instance (right), confidence climbs steadily and crosses the upper threshold, ending the chain once the model is confident enough.

Calibrating the thresholds (risk control)

Given the target and a validation set of examples, the two thresholds are selected by distribution-free risk control so the true error rate on unseen data stays at or below with high probability. That error rate is not raw accuracy but the validation mean of a per-instance loss in . Writing for the model’s answer at step and for the correct one, with the exit step that induces on example , the risk is

The two thresholds plug in different losses. The upper one fires only when confidence has cleared (so the rule stops) and the answer is wrong — a false positive:

The lower one is its opposite, a false negative that fires when the rule gives up () on an instance some later step, up to the budget horizon , would have answered correctly:

Both losses need the full reasoning trace and the gold answer, so calibration runs offline on labeled data. How that error rate is estimated from a finite validation set is what decides whether the guarantee actually holds:

  • Naive plug-in (the paper’s “no finite-sample correction”) keeps every threshold whose empirical validation risk — computed in a single pass over — is at or below the user’s target . On a finite, and here deliberately small (), validation set that empirical risk is an optimistic estimate of the true risk, so the selected thresholds overfit . Across the 40 random validation/test resamples the mean test risk stays controlled, but its per-resample spread crosses often enough that an individual run violates the target.

  • UCB (concentration-based upper confidence bound) thresholds an upper bound on the risk rather than the point estimate. For a loss bounded in and a chosen failure probability , Hoeffding’s inequality gives, for a fixed signal-threshold pair,

    so is the confidence level; calibration keeps only thresholds whose bounded risk clears . The correction term inflates when the validation size is small and vanishes as grows, so the conservativeness adapts to how much data backs the estimate.

  • Scanning many candidates is not a separate method but an additional correction to UCB: the Hoeffding bound holds for one fixed , so sweeping many signals and thresholds invites multiple-comparison inflation. A union bound over the candidate grid — the set of all pairs being searched — would correct it, replacing with . The paper flags this but uses the plain single-candidate correction and reports realized risk on a held-out test set.

In the two-threshold setting the single target splits in two, and the thresholds are calibrated in two decoupled steps rather than one joint search over pairs: UCB first selects against an upper target , then — with fixed — the lower-threshold shape is selected against a lower target . The second step still controls risk because is already locked. A fully joint search (via learn-then-test) is possible, but the authors found the decoupled procedure works as well in practice, at some loss of theoretical rigor.

Choosing a signal (efficiency loss)

Risk control rarely returns a single answer — for a given , every signal-and-threshold pair whose UCB-corrected risk clears the budget is feasible, and usually several do. The efficiency loss is the tie-breaking objective: it scores how many tokens a configuration wastes, normalized by the total budget , and does not itself depend on the calibration. Two forms target the two thresholds:

  • Upper-threshold loss is normalized regret — the fraction of the budget spent reasoning after the answer was already right:

    where is the oracle stopping step, the first one whose answer is correct.

  • Lower-threshold loss counts wasted deliberation instead — the fraction of steps so far whose answer was still wrong, which approaches when a long run never makes progress:

  • Selection averages the per-instance loss over the validation set and keeps the feasible candidate that minimizes it:

    with the exit step of the th sample. Across the candidate signals this yields an ensemble that selects the cheapest signal-and-threshold for each target risk and dataset.

Results

The authors evaluate on four reasoning models — Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and the vision-language model Qwen3-VL-8B — across AIME (1983–2025), a subset of DeepScaleR with AIME removed, GPQA-Diamond, and the vision benchmark MathVision. Generation uses each model card’s recommended decoding settings under vLLM. The four stopping signals from Methods are compared. Thresholds are calibrated over 40 random validation-test splits with a validation set of 50 samples (5 percent), sweeping from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.01. Two things are measured: whether the achieved test risk stays under (control), and how many questions the model answers correctly against the total tokens spent (efficiency).

  • Finite-sample correction keeps risk on target (Figure 4): with the UCB correction, the achieved risk on the held-out test set stays at or below the user-specified across the 40 splits. The naive plug-in keeps the mean risk controlled, but its variance bands routinely cross the line, so individual runs exceed the target.
  • The ensemble picks the most efficient signal per risk level (Figure 5): selecting the signal-threshold pair with the lowest efficiency loss on validation transfers to a better accuracy-versus-token trade-off on test than any single fixed signal. On Qwen3-8B, where the trained probe is one of the four candidate signals, the ensemble selects it over the other three (confidence, EAT, token count) at essentially every risk level — the probe is simply the most efficient signal there.
  • The lower threshold pays off when unsolvable instances are common (Figure 6): on pooled AIME and GPQA-Diamond sets with controlled solvable-to-unsolvable ratios, the upper-only rule clusters at the high-token end because many runs never reach the confidence cutoff and run to the budget limit. Adding the lower threshold shifts the accuracy-versus-token curve toward fewer tokens at similar accuracy, and the gain grows as the solvable-to-unsolvable ratio shifts from 3:1 to 1:3. At a representative operating point, solvable instances tend to exit via the upper threshold and unsolvable ones via the lower threshold, matching the design intent.

My Notes

  • Standard risk control applied to a new quantity: the machinery is the usual distribution-free risk control [5] (Learn-then-Test and risk-controlling prediction sets), which turns any black-box score into one with a finite-sample guarantee. The closest LLM precedent, Conformal Language Modeling [6], calibrated a stopping rule over a set of sampled candidates so the returned set provably contains an acceptable answer. This paper instead calibrates when to stop a single reasoning chain, trading error rate against compute.
  • A rising floor turns the stop test into a rate-of-progress check: a static lower threshold would fire only when confidence drops, which rarely happens on a stuck run, where confidence tends to sit flat and low. Because the floor instead climbs with the budget, the question becomes whether confidence is rising fast enough rather than whether it is high enough right now. That is what lets the rule abandon instances whose confidence never improves. It is calibrated giving-up that sidesteps metacognition: it reads the trajectory from outside and imposes a schedule, never judging whether the question is answerable, which is exactly the judgment AbstentionBench [7] finds reasoning models make poorly.
  • CROP applies the same risk control to a finished trace: CROP [8] runs after the trace is generated, certifying the longest leading prefix whose step-risk proxies all stay below a calibrated threshold and routing the uncertified suffix to repair. Conformal Thinking instead runs during generation, calibrating stop/continue thresholds against a compute budget. Both fix a single threshold off a step-level signal under exchangeability.
  • The guarantee rests on exchangeability: the framework inherits conformal prediction’s core assumption that calibration and test data are exchangeable, and the paper’s own ablations show that is where it strains. False-negative control from the lower threshold degrades under a shift from short to long reasoning horizons, and the size of the efficiency gain depends on the solvable-to-unsolvable mix of the test set. A production query stream that drifts away from the calibration set would weaken the risk guarantee with no visible signal that the target is no longer being met.

References

  1. Wang, X., Suresh, A., Zhang, A., More, R., Jurayj, W., Van Durme, B., Farajtabar, M., Khashabi, D., and Nalisnick, E. “Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) (arXiv:2602.03814), February 3, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03814
  2. Yang, C., Si, Q., Duan, Y., Zhu, Z., Zhu, C., Li, Q., Chen, M., Lin, Z., and Wang, W. “Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2504.15895), 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15895
  3. Wang, Y., Zhang, Y., Yu, T., Xu, C., Zhang, F., and Lian, F. “Adaptive Deep Reasoning: Triggering Deep Thinking When Needed.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2505.20101), 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20101
  4. Zhang, A., Chen, Y., Pan, J., Zhao, C., Panda, A., Li, J., and He, H. “Reasoning Models Know When They’re Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2504.05419), 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05419
  5. Angelopoulos, A. N. and Bates, S. “A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2107.07511), July 2021. Published as Conformal Prediction: A Gentle Introduction, Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 16(4): 494–591, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07511
  6. Quach, V., Fisch, A., Schuster, T., Yala, A., Sohn, J. H., Jaakkola, T. S., and Barzilay, R. “Conformal Language Modeling.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) (arXiv:2306.10193), 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10193
  7. Kirichenko, P., Ibrahim, M., Chaudhuri, K., and Bell, S. J. “AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions.” NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (arXiv:2506.09038). https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038
  8. Cheung, M. Y., Veeraraghavan, A., Chen, H., and Balakrishnan, G. “Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.30085), May 28, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30085

Related Posts

  • Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes — the other way to put conformal risk control on a reasoning trace: instead of choosing when to stop generating, it certifies the longest leading slice of a finished trace that provably contains no error. Both calibrate a single threshold off a step-level signal under exchangeability.
  • A Primer on Conformal Prediction — the distribution-free risk-control machinery (Learn-then-Test, risk-controlling prediction sets) that the calibration step here rests on.
  • Conformal Language Modeling — the closest LLM precedent, calibrating a stopping rule over a set of sampled candidates rather than along a single reasoning trajectory.
  • AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions — the abstention angle the lower threshold sidesteps: reasoning models judge answerability poorly, while the lower threshold gives up from outside the model without any such judgment.
  • Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning — both measure progress as a slope, at different scales: the lower threshold here reads a rate of progress within a single trace (confidence against tokens spent), while that post wanted a cross-system version and found no shared x-axis to define one on.

item.title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems [1] (arXiv preprint, April 2026), Jiacheng Liu, Xiaohan Zhao, Xinyi Shang, and Zhiqiang Shen (MBZUAI + UCL) reverse-engineer the published TypeScript of Claude Code and trace its architecture from five stated values down to specific source files.

Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that can run shell commands, edit files, and call external services on behalf of the user. This study describes its comprehensive architecture by analyzing the publicly available TypeScript source code and further comparing it with OpenClaw, an independent open-source AI agent system that answers many of the same design questions from a different deployment context. Our analysis identifies five human values, philosophies, and needs that motivate the architecture (human decision authority, safety and security, reliable execution, capability amplification, and contextual adaptability) and traces them through thirteen design principles to specific implementation choices. The core of the system is a simple while-loop that calls the model, runs tools, and repeats. Most of the code, however, lives in the systems around this loop: a permission system with seven modes and an ML-based classifier, a five-layer compaction pipeline for context management, four extensibility mechanisms (MCP, plugins, skills, and hooks), a subagent delegation mechanism with worktree isolation, and append-oriented session storage. A comparison with OpenClaw, a multi-channel personal assistant gateway, shows that the same recurring design questions produce different architectural answers when the deployment context changes: from per-action safety classification to perimeter-level access control, from a single CLI loop to an embedded runtime within a gateway control plane, and from context-window extensions to gateway-wide capability registration. We finally identify six open design directions for future agent systems, grounded in recent empirical, architectural, and policy literature.

How the paper reads the code

The paper is a source-level reverse-engineering, not an empirical study. The authors extract the TypeScript of Claude Code v2.1.88 from its published npm package, read it directly, and compare it against OpenClaw, an open-source multi-channel assistant that answers the same design questions in a different deployment context. To keep an analysis of closed, minified code honest, every claim is tagged with one of three evidence tiers:

  • Tier A (product-documented): drawn from Anthropic’s official documentation and engineering posts.
  • Tier B (code-verified): tied to specific files and functions in the extracted v2.1.88 source. The paper treats this as its strongest tier.
  • Tier C (reconstructed): inferred from code patterns, community analysis, or the OpenClaw comparison, and explicitly marked as inference.

The analysis is built around a few recurring design questions put to any agent system: where reasoning lives, how many execution engines run, what the default safety posture is, and what the binding resource constraint is. Claude Code’s answers are traced through source files, then organized into a chain from values to principles to implementation.

Five values, thirteen principles

The paper reads five human values as motivating the architecture: human decision authority, safety and security, reliable execution, capability amplification, and contextual adaptability. Those values are traced through thirteen design principles to concrete code. Table 1 lists the thirteen, the values each serves, and the design-space question each answers.

A sixth concern is kept separate from the five, used as an evaluative lens rather than a design driver: whether the architecture preserves long-term human capability. The authors note this is not prominent in Anthropic’s stated values, but flag it because the evidence is real. They cite a “paradox of supervision,” where over-reliance on the agent erodes the skills needed to supervise it, and a study finding developers in AI-assisted conditions score 17% lower on comprehension tests.

Seven components, five layers

The architecture is deliberately lopsided. Figure 1 (the cover) gives the high-level shape: seven functional components (the user, the interfaces, the agent loop, the permission system, the tools, state and persistence, and the execution environment), with every entry point feeding into one agent loop at the center. The reasoning lives entirely in the model, reached through that single loop, so the loop itself is close to trivial: call the model, run any tools it requests, feed the results back, repeat until it stops asking for tools. Almost all of the code is in the systems wrapped around the loop, which the paper sorts into five layers:

  • Surface layer: entry points (the interactive and headless CLIs, the Agent SDK, IDE and browser front-ends) and rendering.
  • Core layer: the agent loop and the compaction pipeline.
  • Safety/action layer: the permission system and its auto-mode classifier, the hook pipeline, extensibility, built-in and MCP tools, the shell sandbox, and subagent spawning.
  • State layer: context assembly, runtime state, session persistence, the CLAUDE.md and memory hierarchy, and sidechain transcripts.
  • Backend layer: execution backends and external resources.

One turn through the loop

A single turn is a fixed pipeline in query.ts, written as an async generator so output streams to the interface while control flow stays single-threaded. The prompt enters through context assembly, the model is called, each tool request passes the permission gate (allow, ask, or deny, with deny feedback looped back to the model), results return, and the loop repeats until a turn produces no tool use and the assistant replies. The paper fills in the mechanics:

  • Tool dispatch is concurrent-read, serial-write: read-only calls run in parallel as they stream in, state-modifying calls like shell commands are serialized, and results are buffered and returned in the order the model requested them. If one Bash call errors, a sibling abort controller kills the other in-flight subprocesses.
  • Five context shapers run in sequence before every model call, cheapest first: budget reduction (caps oversized tool results), snip (trims old history), microcompact (fine-grained, cache-aware compression), context collapse (a read-time projection that hides summarized history without deleting it), and auto-compact (a full model-generated summary, fired only if the context still exceeds the pressure threshold after the other four).
  • Recovery is layered too: escalate the output-token cap up to three times a turn, reactive compaction near capacity, prompt-too-long handling that tries overflow recovery before giving up, a streaming fallback, and a fallback model.
  • Stop conditions: a turn ends on text with no tool use (the normal case), a max-turns limit, context overflow, a PostToolUse hook halting continuation, or an explicit abort.

The loop is reactive, in the ReAct style: each turn runs one action sequence with no backtracking, trading search completeness for simplicity and latency.

Permission and safety

Every tool call passes a permission gate before it runs. The default posture is deny-first with human escalation: deny rules override ask rules override allow rules, and an unrecognized action is escalated to the user rather than run silently. Seven permission modes span a graduated autonomy spectrum from plan (approve every plan first) through default and acceptEdits to bypassPermissions. The authorization pipeline runs pre-filtering, a PreToolUse hook, rule evaluation, then the permission handler, and an auto-mode machine-learning classifier adds a two-stage fast filter plus a chain-of-thought safety judgment on each call. Shell commands run in a sandbox. Because reasoning and enforcement sit on separate code paths, a compromised or adversarially manipulated model cannot override the sandbox, the permission checks, or the deny-first rules in the harness.

Four ways to extend the loop

The four extension mechanisms attach at different points of the loop and cost different amounts of context:

  • Hooks: intercept the tool lifecycle (zero context cost).
  • Skills: inject domain instructions (low cost).
  • Plugins: bundle components for distribution (medium cost).
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): connect external tool servers (high cost).

The paper’s reading is that no single mechanism can span the range from a zero-context lifecycle hook to a schema-heavy tool server without forcing trade-offs on extension authors. The graduated cost ordering lets cheap extensions scale widely while the expensive ones are reserved for cases that genuinely need new tools.

Context and memory

The context window (200K tokens on older models, 1M on the Claude 4.6 series) is named as the binding constraint, and the memory design is built around it. Figure 6 lays out the sources that converge on the window, grouped into six layers and ordered by how mutable each is and when it loads.

The layers run from a read-only system layer (system prompt, environment info, output styles, MCP tool names) loaded at startup, through hot-reloading project config (the five-level CLAUDE.md hierarchy and path-scoped rules), a memory layer (auto memory and the compact summary that replaces long history), the conversation itself (history and subagent summaries), runtime state appended during the turn (file reads, command outputs, tool results), and a lazy on-demand layer (deferred tool definitions pulled in via ToolSearch only when needed). The window is therefore not fixed at assembly time but grows as the turn runs.

The compaction pipeline has five layers because no single strategy covers every kind of context pressure. Budget reduction targets individual oversized tool outputs, snip handles temporal depth, microcompact reacts to cache overhead, context collapse manages very long histories, and auto-compact does semantic compression as a last resort. Each layer operates at a different cost-benefit point, and the cheaper ones run first.

Subagents and session storage

A subagent is spawned through the same tool factory as everything else, re-entering the query loop with its own isolated context window and permission scope, optionally inside a git worktree. Only its final response text returns to the parent. The full subagent history never enters the parent’s window, which keeps the parent’s context cheap.

Session storage is append-only (history, sidechains, checkpoints), favoring auditability over query power. Resume and fork restore messages but deliberately not session-scoped permissions, so a resumed session does not silently inherit trust the user granted earlier.

Claude Code versus OpenClaw

The OpenClaw contrast is the part that generalizes. OpenClaw is a local-first WebSocket gateway daemon that connects roughly two dozen messaging channels (WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Signal, and others) to an embedded agent runtime. Where Claude Code is an ephemeral per-session CLI coding harness bound to one repository, OpenClaw is a persistent control plane for multi-channel personal assistance. Posed the same six design questions, it answers them differently because its deployment context differs. Table 3 lines them up:

Dimension Claude Code OpenClaw
System scope CLI/IDE coding harness; ephemeral per-session process Persistent WebSocket gateway daemon; multi-channel control plane
Trust model Deny-first per-action rule evaluation with hooks and an optional ML classifier; seven permission modes; graduated trust spectrum Single trusted operator per gateway; DM pairing and allowlists for inbound channels; opt-in sandboxing with configurable scope and multiple backends
Agent runtime Iterative async generator (queryLoop()) as the system center Agent runner embedded inside the gateway’s RPC dispatch; per-session queue serialization
Extension architecture Four mechanisms at graduated context costs: MCP, plugins, skills, hooks Manifest-first plugin system with twelve capability types and a central registry; separate skills layer; built-in MCP
Memory and context CLAUDE.md four-level hierarchy; five-layer compaction pipeline; LLM-based memory scan Workspace bootstrap files; a separate memory system (daily notes, optional “dreaming” for long-term promotion); auto-compaction with pluggable providers; optional hybrid vector + keyword search
Multi-agent and routing Task-delegating subagents (Explore, Plan, general-purpose); worktree isolation; only the final response returns to the parent Multi-agent routing with isolated agents and channel dispatch, plus sub-agent delegation with configurable nesting depth

The trust boundary is in different places. Claude Code puts it between the model and the execution environment, while OpenClaw puts it at the gateway perimeter, assuming a single trusted operator and explicitly not supporting hostile multi-tenant isolation. Claude Code’s extensions change what one agent can do, while OpenClaw’s plugins add capabilities across every agent on the gateway. The two are not purely alternatives: OpenClaw can host Claude Code (and OpenAI Codex, and Gemini CLI) as an external coding harness through its Agent Client Protocol integration, so they stack.

What the analysis concludes

The discussion reads the architecture as a set of consistent choices rather than a grab-bag:

  • Minimal scaffolding, rich harness: the system invests in deterministic infrastructure (context management, tool routing, recovery) instead of decision scaffolding like explicit planners or state graphs, on the premise that a more capable model gains more from a rich operating environment than from a framework that constrains its choices.
  • Graduated layering over single switches: permission modes, compaction layers, and extension points are all spectrums rather than one-shot mechanisms.
  • Append-only over queryable: state favors an auditable log over a mutable store that would be easier to query.
  • Model judgment inside a deterministic harness: probabilistic guidance (CLAUDE.md) is kept on a separate code path from deterministic enforcement (permission rules).
  • A trust trajectory, not a fixed state: autonomy is “co-constructed” over time, with auto-approve rates rising from about 20% under 50 sessions to over 40% by 750, so the design targets a relationship that loosens as trust builds.
  • What it deliberately does not do: no planning graph imposed on the model, no single unified extension mechanism, and no full restore of session-scoped trust state on resume.

The paper also names four standing tensions it does not claim to resolve: safety versus autonomy, the permission model under adversarial conditions, context efficiency versus transparency, and simplicity versus extensibility.

Six open directions

The paper closes with six open directions for future agent systems: the observability and silent-failure gap, cross-session persistence and longer-term memory, evolution of the harness boundary (where, when, and what the agent acts on), horizon scaling from a single session to a longer program of work, governance and oversight at scale, and a long-term-human-capability lens for judging these systems.

References

  1. Liu, Jiacheng, Zhao, Xiaohan, Shang, Xinyi, Shen, Zhiqiang. “Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.14228), April 14, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14228

  • Where Claude Code Tokens Go: the outside-the-tool measurement of the context cost that the paper’s compaction pipeline is built to manage.
  • A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds: a real instance of the single-destructive-call failure mode the per-action permission gate is meant to catch.
  • Snowflake Cortex AI Escapes Sandbox and Executes Malware: another agent-safety boundary failure, a counterpoint to the deny-first “untrusted model on a trusted machine” posture.
