item.title: Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate [1], Keramati et al. (UC Irvine) show that the confidence of an LLM’s first few generated tokens predicts how a judge rates the quality of its reasoning in a debate-based essay-scoring system, often better than statistics taken over the whole response.

Evaluating reasoning quality in multi-agent LLM systems is challenging, especially for open-ended tasks without reference answers. We investigate whether intrinsic confidence signals, token-level log-probabilities from decoding, can predict reasoning quality as assessed by LLM-as-judge evaluation. Using a debate-based essay scoring framework, we compare confidence proxies against rubric-based judge scores across two ASAP essay sets. We find that early-token confidence, particularly within the first few generated tokens, is consistently the strongest predictor of reasoning quality, outperforming full-sequence statistics. Analysis of log-probability trajectories shows that the opening phase of generation is the most heterogeneous and therefore most informative. We also observe a systematic asymmetry between agent roles, with stronger alignment between confidence and quality for supportive reasoning than for adversarial critique. These results suggest that early decoding dynamics provide a lightweight and effective signal for estimating reasoning reliability in multi-agent LLM systems.

Methods

The framework scores essays through a structured debate, then mines the debaters’ own decoding signals rather than any reference answer:

  • Two debating agents: an Advocate argues an essay’s strengths against a rubric trait and a Skeptic rebuts with limitations, both producing open-ended argument without assigning a score. Both are generated by GPT-4o-mini.
  • Confidence signals: during decoding, each agent’s per-token log-probabilities are recorded as an intrinsic confidence trace over the response.
  • Windows and statistics: from each trace they extract a handful of candidate windows anchored at the start or end of the response — the first or last tokens (a fixed count; the paper’s features span of 3, 5, 10, and 30) and the first or last tokens (a fraction of the response length , e.g. the final half) — plus the full response, and summarize each window by its mean, median, min, max, variance, standard deviation, range, and trajectory slope.
  • LLM-as-judge targets: a separate GPT-5-mini judge reads the debate transcript and scores each argument on five targets, which the confidence statistics are then tested against:
    • Instruction following — three-point ordinal (1 = Low, 2 = Medium, 3 = High)
    • Justification quality — three-point ordinal
    • Evidence grounding — three-point ordinal
    • Aggregate score — the composite, in
    • Critical failure — a binary flag for a severe error; when it fires, the aggregate score above is overridden to 0 Prediction quality is measured per target by its natural metric: Spearman’s (and Kendall’s ) for the four ordinal targets, AUROC for the binary critical-failure flag. So “critical-failure detection” is just the binary-classification slice of the analysis — predicting that flag — as opposed to rank-correlating the ordinal scores.

Results

The data is the ASAP automated-essay-scoring benchmark (the Hewlett Foundation’s Automated Student Assessment Prize), restricted to Essay Sets 7 and 8 (the only sets with trait-level human annotations). Advocate and Skeptic arguments come from GPT-4o-mini, and the judge is a deterministic GPT-5-mini. Table 1 reports, for each role–target pair, the top three confidence features ranked by their fit to the judge score and the best score achieved.

Early-token confidence is the standout predictor, most clearly for catching severe failures and on the harder essay set:

  • Critical-failure detection is strong. The max of the first 3 tokens reaches AUROC 0.849 for the Advocate on Set 7, and the median of the first 5 tokens reaches 0.759 on Set 8, so severe errors tend to show up as localized confidence spikes or drops right at the opening.
  • Fine-grained quality ranking is weak. The best Spearman correlations with ordinal scores top out near 0.39 (Advocate, Set 7), and the Skeptic’s barely reach 0.11 to 0.27.
  • Roles are asymmetric. Confidence aligns with judged quality far better for the supportive Advocate than the adversarial Skeptic, across both sets.
  • Not uniformly early-token. On Set 7 the Advocate’s best ordinal predictor was the full-response median, not an opening-window feature. The early-token advantage shows up mainly on Set 8 and for critical-failure detection.

The judge leans hard on its top score — it assigns a 3 to 77% of essays on instruction following, 79% on justification quality, and 93% on evidence grounding. Evidence grounding is so saturated it behaves almost like a constant, which leaves little rank variation for any confidence feature to align with and mechanically holds its correlation down — a ceiling in the labels, not a failure of the signal.

My Notes

  • Intrinsic confidence works for open-ended reasoning too. Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know established that a model’s token probabilities track correctness on closed-form tasks. This paper extends the idea to open-ended, reference-free reasoning and localizes it: the first three to five tokens hold more predictive signal than the full sequence, which makes the proxy a cheap decoding-time read rather than a separate calibration model [1].
  • Confidence is diagnostic for advocacy, not for critique. The Skeptic’s log-probability confidence barely correlates with judged quality (Spearman 0.11 to 0.27) while the Advocate’s does (up to 0.39, AUROC 0.85). That matches a known soft spot: MAST found verification failures — a system not checking its own work — to be a recurring multi-agent breakdown. Here the critique role is also where intrinsic confidence is least informative, so monitoring helps least on the function that most needs a second look.
  • It is a failure flag, not a fine scorer. Rank agreement with graded quality is weak (Spearman around 0.39 at best), but critical-failure detection is strong (AUROC up to 0.85). And the abstract’s “consistently the strongest” is set-dependent: on Essay Set 7 the Advocate’s best ordinal predictor was the full-response median, not an early-token feature.
  • What can we do with token logits reliably? Only one thing transfers across the paper’s two essay sets: the predictive signal lives in the opening three to five tokens, so early-token statistics make a cheap decode-time screen for severe failures (AUROC up to 0.85 within a set). The specific feature and its direction do not transfer — the top detector is the max of the first three tokens on Set 7 but the median of the first five on Set 8, and the signs even disagree (a confident early spike flags failure, a wide early spread suppresses it). So the reliable recipe is narrow: read the first few tokens, but fit which statistic and which sign on your own data rather than lifting a fixed rule from this paper.

References

  1. Keramati, A., Cheok, J., Horne, J., and Warschauer, M. “Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.10307), June 9, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10307

Related Posts

  • MAST: A Failure Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems: the failure-mode map for multi-agent debate that this paper’s critical-failure flag tries to catch cheaply from decoding signals.
  • Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know: the calibration result this paper extends from closed-form correctness to open-ended, reference-free reasoning quality.
  • Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy: another intrinsic, decoding-time uncertainty signal for output quality, against which early-token log-probability is the lighter-weight alternative.
  • SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?: a counterpoint on whether a model’s stated confidence reflects its internal distribution, where this paper reads the distribution directly from log-probabilities instead.

item.title: Pramaana Labs Raises $27M to Bring Formal Verification to AI
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

TechCrunch reports that Pramaana Labs has raised a $27M seed round led by Khosla Ventures to apply formal verification, specifically the Lean proof language used to check mathematical proofs, as a deterministic layer on top of an LLM. The LLM still answers the natural-language question. A Lean-style system then checks that the answer obeys a formalized rulebook. Pramaana is targeting rule-dense, high-stakes verticals like law, tax preparation, and drug discovery, building a separate verification system per domain with oversight from experts such as former IRS commissioner Danny Werfel. The company was founded by three IIT Madras alumni whose backgrounds run through Google Maps moderation, Glean, and Google DeepMind’s Gemini team. Co-founder Ranjan Rajagopalan frames the bet this way: “The world’s hardest problems are not unsolvable. They are unformalized.”

What Pramaana is building:

  • The verification stack. A Domain Formalizer converts regulatory, statutory, and scientific text into machine-checkable specifications, capturing definitions, conditions, exceptions, and dependencies. Provers and solvers then return proof artifacts, proofs, counterexamples, and traceable explanations, showing which rule was used and where the answer follows or fails.
  • Tax first. The opening vertical formalizes tax rules for compliance, advisory, and policy simulation, with legal compliance, clinical safety, software and protocol correctness, and public policy named as later targets.
  • An outside-research arm. A fellowship, Project 1729, invites external teams to formalize high-stakes domains, offering funding, compute, and an embedded Pramaana engineer.

My Notes

  • The bottleneck moves from the model to the spec. The deterministic layer checks that the LLM’s output obeys a formalized rulebook, but it cannot check that the rulebook itself is correct or complete. A proof of conformance is only as good as the formalization, and turning law or tax into Lean means making thousands of interpretive choices that can each be wrong. Verified Doesn’t Mean Nothing Can Go Wrong is the direct caution here: a Claude agent found a buffer overflow in the Lean runtime under code that was itself formally verified.

  • The verticals are rule-dense, but not equally formalizable. Law and tax are good fits because they are written rules, and France’s CATALA project already turns much of the French tax and benefit code into executable form. Drug discovery is a harder case: much of it is empirical and statistical rather than a codified rulebook, so the pitch that codifying the rules makes the reasoning deterministic fits tax far better than it fits biology. The ongoing cost is also real, since a formalization of the tax code has to be re-checked every time the code changes.

  • This is a per-domain build, not a horizontal product. Each vertical gets its own Lean-style system overseen by domain experts: a former IRS commissioner for tax, named professors for cybersecurity and drug discovery. The defensibility comes from the formalization work and the expert relationships, which reads closer to a high-end services model than to software that scales by adding users. The Project 1729 fellowship, which embeds a Pramaana engineer with each outside team, fits that shape: each new domain is its own formalization project. The same LLM-plus-Lean toolchain is being pushed on open math problems in Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search, where the binding constraint is likewise how much gets formalized, not the model.

  • The competitive landscape, especially in law and tax. The field splits on what makes a high-stakes answer trustworthy, and Pramaana’s wager is on machine-checkable proof:

    • The proof camp (Pramaana’s own): Axiom, founder Carina Hong’s Lean-based startup, runs the same deterministic-formal-layer thesis aimed at mathematics. Imandra sells “reasoning as a service,” applying automated reasoning and formal verification to mission-critical and financial-regulatory decisions, which puts it closest to Pramaana’s professional territory.
    • The retrieval camp (what Pramaana positions against): X’s Moonshot for Specialized Professional Intelligence and Harvey chase the legal market with LLM analysis over private documents, while Thomson Reuters and LexisNexis tools still hallucinate more than 17% of the time. In tax, Black Ore’s “Tax Autopilot” automates tax preparation for CPA (certified public accountant) firms with a claimed 99% accuracy, and France’s CATALA remains the closest formal precedent.

Related Posts

  • “Verified” Doesn’t Mean “Nothing Can Go Wrong”: the direct caution for Pramaana’s pitch, where a bug turned up under formally-verified Lean code, showing verification bounds failure but does not eliminate it.
  • Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning: the closest peer, where Axiom makes the same bet as Pramaana, a deterministic formal-reasoning layer under a probabilistic LLM, aimed at mathematics rather than professional verticals.
  • AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 Queries: the reliability problem in the legal vertical Pramaana targets, and a caution on “hallucination-free” reliability claims.
  • Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search: the same LLM-plus-Lean approach applied to open math problems, where formalization is again the limiting factor.
  • When Computers Write Proofs, What’s the Point of Mathematicians?: the older case for Lean-style formalization and what it does and does not capture about human reasoning.

This Long Run Sunday I ran an accidental HM, and it was my 84th!

My goal was to just run 10mi, because I already ran ~14mi two days ago to Alki beach, and 7mi yesterday including my 103rd parkrun. Plan was simple: 4mi run to a nearby McDonald’s to get my ice cream and iced coffee fix, and then wander around until I hit 10mi!

But what do you know, runners? Next moment you realize you’re deep in the woods, and the weather and the world were just too wonderful to stop! I ended up running into Redmond Watershed Preserve, which I’d never properly run through before. So this time I did!

All told, the damage done was 14.40mi with moving time 2:28:23 pace 10’18”/mi, and EG 1,269ft! And I closed this week with the highest weekly mileage and EG year-to-date: 69.45mi and 3,793ft!

But who cares — those beautiful sights are part of my happy memories now! 🙂

Oh and happy summer and happy father’s day!

item.title: Estonia Intends to Recognize AI Agents With Digital IDs
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The Register reports that Estonia plans to give AI agents their own digital identities, so an agent acting for a person can be verified and audited. The primary source is a statement from the Estonian Government Office: at the second meeting of the Eesti.ai advisory board on 17 June 2026, the board agreed to move forward with digital identities for AI agents, which it calls an “AI ID.” Prime Minister Kristen Michal put the goal in terms of one question:

In the future, AI will increasingly carry out digital tasks on our behalf, compiling reports, preparing declarations or interacting with information systems. To that end, it must be clear who is acting on whose behalf with what rights, and who is ultimately responsible.

What the proposal says:

  • Scoped, controllable authority. An agent acting for a person or company is given limited and controllable powers, instead of the person granting an AI assistant access to all of their rights, services, and data.
  • Per-action permissioning. The statement is concrete about granularity: it must be possible to specify whether an agent may only view data, prepare a document, draw up a payment, or act solely within a set financial limit.
  • Built on the existing e-state. The government positions the AI ID as the next layer on the trust infrastructure that already runs the country: a national digital identity, the X-Road data-exchange layer, and legally binding digital signatures.
  • A commitment, with the mechanics still open. This is an agreement to proceed, reached at an advisory-board meeting. The authorization and delegation mechanics are not defined, and the “first country in the world” claim is conditional on acting “quickly, and smartly.”

The Register places the move in a wider scramble over who answers for an agent’s actions. Argentina’s president Javier Milei has endorsed “non-human corporations” run by software with limited liability. In commerce, Target’s terms now treat actions by an agent you authorized as transactions you made, while American Express goes the other way and promises to cover customers when an authorized agent makes a purchase in error. The piece also revives the line from IBM’s 1979 training manual, that a computer can never be held accountable and so must never make a management decision, and notes that courts are filling the gap anyway, holding Air Canada liable for bad chatbot advice.

My Notes

  • A digital ID is really about who to blame. A software agent can’t be punished the way a person can, as Mark Riedl and Deven Desai point out: you can fine or jail a human, not a piece of software. So an AI ID doesn’t make the agent answerable. It records who authorized the agent and how much it was allowed to do, so there is finally a clear human to hold responsible when something goes wrong. The commerce terms above are early, ad hoc stabs at the same problem. A national identity layer would settle it the same way every time.

  • Estonia can be first because the hard part is already built. The AI ID is an increment on e-Estonia’s digital identity, X-Road data exchange, and digital signatures, not a greenfield project. The same fact makes the “first country” claim credible and the approach hard to copy elsewhere: a state without an e-government foundation would have to stand up the identity layer before it could scope an agent’s powers at all.

Related Posts

  • A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds: the harm case that per-action scoping is meant to prevent, an agent with unscoped authority taking a catastrophic, state-changing action.
  • Policy on the AI Exponential: Dario Amodei’s argument that policy is outrun by capability. Estonia is a government moving early, at the identity-infrastructure layer rather than the model layer.
  • OpenAI’s Five Principles for AGI: private labs publishing voluntary values statements, in contrast to a state building enforceable identity and permission infrastructure for agents.
  • The Core Challenges Facing Agentic AI Today: the capability backdrop to delegating real authority, why handing autonomous agents open-ended tasks was already fraught before they could spend money on your behalf.

item.title: Spiking Neural Networks: A Primer
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are often called the “third generation” of neural network models, a term due to Maass [2], after the McCulloch–Pitts threshold unit [3] and the continuous-valued, rate-based units of modern deep learning. The idea is older than the name: the integrate-and-fire neuron goes back to Lapicque in 1907, Hodgkin and Huxley’s 1952 model of the action potential [4] earned a Nobel Prize, and computing with spikes drew sustained interest through the 1990s before energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware revived it in the 2010s. The defining difference: SNN neurons communicate with discrete, asynchronous, binary events called spikes placed in continuous time, rather than with real-valued activations exchanged synchronously layer by layer. Computation becomes a function not just of which neurons fire and how much, but of when they fire.

Research questions and goals

The field is pulled by three partly-overlapping agendas, and which one a given paper serves matters, because the three imply different success criteria.

  1. Energy-efficient computation. Spikes are sparse and event-driven: a neuron does work only when it receives or emits a spike, and a multiply-accumulate collapses to an accumulate (no weight is multiplied by a graded activation, just an accumulate when a spike arrives). On the right hardware this promises orders-of-magnitude lower energy than dense matrix multiplication. The central question is whether that advantage holds on real tasks at competitive accuracy.

  2. Computational neuroscience. SNNs are the natural modeling substrate for how biological brains actually compute, since real neurons spike. Here the goal is explanatory: understanding coding, plasticity, and dynamics. Biological plausibility is a feature rather than a constraint to relax.

  3. Temporal computation. Because state and timing are intrinsic, SNNs are a candidate substrate for streaming, event-based, low-latency signals (event cameras, audio, sensor streams) where the input is naturally a sparse stream of events rather than a sequence of dense frames.

The hard open problem cutting across all three agendas is training. The spike-generating function is a threshold (a step), so its derivative is zero almost everywhere and undefined at threshold, leaving standard backpropagation no gradient to descend. Most methodological research of the last decade is, directly or indirectly, an answer to a handful of open questions:

  • The non-differentiability problem. How do you train a network whose core nonlinearity is a non-differentiable step? The two leading answers are surrogate gradients [1] and conversion from a trained artificial neural network (ANN) [5].
  • What should spikes encode? Rate, precise timing, or something in between? Does that choice change what the network can compute, and how cheaply?
  • Can learning be local and online? Global backpropagation-through-time [6] works but is biologically implausible and awkward for hardware. The leading local alternative is spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which adjusts each synapse using only the relative timing of its own pre- and post-synaptic spikes [7], [8]. Today it does not close the gap: unsupervised STDP reaches about 95% on MNIST [9] against the 99%+ of backprop-trained networks, and the gap widens sharply on harder benchmarks, with pure STDP yet to produce competitive results on ImageNet. Whether a local rule can ever match backprop on accuracy is the open question.
  • Can the accuracy gap close without re-importing the cost? SNNs still trail conventional networks on large-scale tasks: on ImageNet the best directly-trained SNNs reach roughly 80% top-1 accuracy against the ~90% of leading conventional models (details below). Closing that gap while keeping the sparsity and energy advantage, rather than reintroducing the dense computation that made conventional networks expensive, is the open engineering question.

Techniques and the mathematics

The neuron model

The most widely used model is the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, whose membrane potential integrates incoming current and leaks back toward rest. It is defined by its rate of change:

You integrate this over time to get , the “integrate” in integrate-and-fire. (The literature usually writes the equivalent form , with the time constant multiplying the derivative.)

In plain terms: the voltage leaks steadily back toward its resting level while incoming current pushes it up. When the push wins and the integrated voltage reaches threshold, the neuron fires and resets.

Here is the input current (the summed synaptic drive) and the membrane resistance, so is the voltage the input would drive the membrane to at rest. When crosses a threshold , the neuron emits a spike and is reset (to or by subtracting ). The constant is the membrane time constant, the timescale over which the voltage relaxes back toward rest once input stops, much like an circuit discharging. A large means a slow leak and a long memory of past input. A small one means the neuron forgets almost immediately and responds only to near-coincident spikes.

For simulation and training this is discretized. A common form, written as a recurrent unit over time steps :

In plain terms: this is the same leaky neuron rewritten so a computer can step through it in time. At each tick it keeps the previous voltage but shrinks it by the decay , adds the new weighted input , and subtracts the threshold to reset if it fired on the last tick.

where is the membrane potential at time step (the discrete-time counterpart of ), the synaptic weights, the input spikes arriving at that step, the decay factor, the output spike, and the Heaviside step function ( when , else ), so the neuron emits a spike () exactly when the potential reaches the threshold and stays silent () below it. The last term subtracts the threshold after a spike, implementing reset-by-subtraction. In this form an SNN is essentially a recurrent network with a binary activation and a built-in leak, which is exactly why deep-learning training methods can be brought to bear.

Other neuron models trade biological fidelity against cost:

  • Hodgkin–Huxley [4] (1952): a system of coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) modeling ion-channel conductances. Biophysically faithful, expensive.
  • Izhikevich [10] (2003): two coupled equations, and with after-spike reset. A celebrated sweet spot: it reproduces a large repertoire of cortical firing patterns (bursting, chattering, fast-spiking) at roughly the cost of LIF.
  • Spike Response Model [11] (Gerstner): an integral, kernel-based reformulation convenient for analysis.

What spikes encode

A spiking network has to commit to what a spike means: how information is read out of a spike train. Rate and temporal/latency coding are the two ends of a spectrum, differing in how much they rely on the precise timing of spikes rather than their average count, and a real code can sit anywhere between them. Population coding is a separate question (which neurons in a group fire) and combines with either. What matters in practice is how a use case maps the code onto the output format it needs:

  • Rate coding → a class label. Each input (say, a pixel) drives a spike train whose rate is proportional to its value, and a downstream neuron’s firing rate then stands in for a real-valued activation (80 spikes in 100 steps ≈ an activation of 0.8). The output layer has one neuron per class, and the prediction is the output neuron with the highest spike count over the window, the spiking analogue of taking an ANN’s largest logit. This is the default for ANN-to-SNN conversion and deep-SNN image classifiers, where accuracy matters more than latency. The cost is the many time steps needed to estimate each rate, and that when spikes occur is discarded.
  • Temporal / latency coding → a fast decision. Information lives in when a neuron first fires: a stronger or more salient input fires earlier (time-to-first-spike). The readout watches for the earliest output spikes and settles on a class as soon as one fires, often before the full window elapses. That is what suits it to ultra-low-latency, low-power inference (always-on keyword spotting or fast detection on neuromorphic chips) and to models of the brain’s rapid visual categorization. It is sparse (potentially one spike per neuron) but harder to train and more fragile.
  • Population coding → a continuous value. Each neuron has a preferred value (a tuning curve), and a quantity is represented by the pattern of activity across the group. The output is decoded as a weighted combination of the population’s firing (a population vector, or a learned linear decoder), yielding a continuous vector rather than a discrete class. This underlies continuous-variable tasks like motor control and robotics: it is the basis of the Neural Engineering Framework [12] behind Nengo, and of the classic decoding of movement direction from motor-cortex activity [13].

Training methods

Three broad families of methods are used to train an SNN.

ANN-to-SNN conversion. Train a conventional rectified-linear-unit (ReLU) network normally, then map activations to firing rates and copy the weights into a rate-coded SNN, calibrating thresholds [5], [14]. Achieves near-ANN accuracy and sidesteps the gradient problem entirely, but typically needs many time steps (high latency, eroding the energy win) and only yields rate codes.

Surrogate gradients. The dominant direct-training approach. Use the hard step on the forward pass, but substitute a smooth surrogate derivative on the backward pass, pretending (only for gradient purposes) that the spike function had a soft slope. A common choice is the derivative of a fast sigmoid [15] or a triangular/boxcar function centered at threshold:

In plain terms: a real spike is all-or-nothing, so its true slope is zero almost everywhere and undefined at threshold, useless for gradient descent. On the backward pass we pretend the neuron responded smoothly, with sensitivity highest right at threshold and tapering off as the voltage moves away from it.

Unrolling the LIF recurrence over time and applying backpropagation-through-time then trains the network end-to-end. This is the core idea behind STBP (spatio-temporal backpropagation) [16] and is surveyed definitively by Neftci, Mostafa & Zenke [1]. The broader set of supervised and unsupervised methods is reviewed by Tavanaei et al. [17].

Local / biologically-inspired plasticity. STDP is an unsupervised, local rule: a synapse strengthens if the presynaptic spike precedes the postsynaptic one (causal, “pre-before-post”) and weakens otherwise. The dependence was characterized experimentally by Markram et al. [8] and Bi & Poo [7]. A standard form:

In plain terms: if the input spike lands just before the neuron fires, the synapse is strengthened (it helped cause the spike). If it lands just after, it is weakened, and either effect fades the further apart in time the two spikes are.

with . STDP needs no labels or global error signal and maps cleanly onto on-chip learning, but on its own it lags supervised methods on accuracy. Diehl & Cook [9] is the canonical demonstration, reaching competitive MNIST accuracy with STDP alone. It remains central to the neuroscience agenda and to online-learning hardware.

How biologically realistic is it, really?

SNNs are routinely described as “more biologically realistic” than conventional networks. That’s true, but in a narrower sense than the phrase suggests, and it’s worth separating what holds from what gets oversold.

The claim holds at the level of signal representation. Real neurons communicate with discrete action potentials whose timing encodes information, and SNNs do the same. Conventional rate-based networks do neither: each unit emits a single continuous value with no temporal structure. SNNs also maintain intrinsic state (membrane potential, leak) and event-driven dynamics that mirror real neural behavior. STDP in particular was discovered experimentally in biology and then imported into SNNs, so that learning rule is genuinely biologically grounded rather than reverse-engineered. By this measure an SNN is unambiguously closer to a brain than a ReLU multilayer perceptron (MLP).

But “more realistic than an ANN” is a low bar, and most working SNNs clear it and then stop:

  • The standard LIF neuron is a gross simplification: a single compartment, no dendritic computation, no ion-channel dynamics, a fixed threshold. Real neurons are closer to small nonlinear networks in themselves. Hodgkin–Huxley is far more biophysically detailed, but its cost and stiff dynamics keep it almost entirely out of trained networks. It lives in computational-neuroscience simulation instead.
  • The most successful SNNs are trained with surrogate-gradient backpropagation-through-time, and backprop is exactly the part that is biologically implausible, since it needs a global error signal, symmetric weight transport, and a backward pass the brain has no obvious mechanism for [18]. The systems that perform best are realistic in their neurons and implausible in their learning.
  • Rate coding, the easiest regime to train, discards the spike-timing information that motivated the realism argument in the first place, leaving a spiking implementation of essentially rate-based computation.
  • Connectivity structure, neuromodulation, glia, conduction delays, the diversity of neuron types: none of it is in a typical SNN.

Biological realism is really an argument for using SNNs in neuroscience rather than in engineering. For the energy and edge-AI agenda the operative property is sparse, event-driven computation on neuromorphic hardware, an efficiency argument rather than a fidelity one. The two get conflated because “brain-like” sells, but a system can be brain-like in the way that matters for power (sparse spikes) while being quite unbrain-like in how it learns.

Potential impact

  • Edge and always-on AI. Ultra-low-power inference for wearables, hearing aids, keyword spotting, and battery-constrained sensors: the most credible near-term commercial case.
  • Event-based vision and robotics. Pairing with event cameras (dynamic vision sensors), which output sparse per-pixel brightness-change events [19], SNNs offer microsecond-latency, low-power perception for drones, autonomous systems, and high-speed tracking.
  • Neuroscience. Large-scale spiking simulations test theories of coding, plasticity, and circuit dynamics, feeding back into our understanding of biological computation.
  • Sustainability. If the energy advantage holds at scale, neuromorphic computing is one of the few proposals that attacks the rising energy cost of AI at the architectural level rather than the process-node level.

Most efficiency claims are realized only on matched neuromorphic hardware. On a graphics processing unit (GPU), simulating an SNN over many time steps is often slower and more energy-hungry than the equivalent conventional network. The advantage is a hardware–algorithm co-design story, not an algorithm-alone story.

Current status

Hardware is the most mature dimension. Intel Loihi 2 (with the open Lava software framework), IBM NorthPole [20], Manchester SpiNNaker 2 [21], Heidelberg BrainScaleS-2 [22], and commercial parts like BrainChip Akida and SynSense processors are all available to researchers or in products. These demonstrate real energy and latency wins on sparse, event-driven workloads.

Software has matured rapidly: snnTorch, Norse, SpikingJelly, BindsNET, and Nengo make surrogate-gradient training routine on top of PyTorch, and standardized event-based datasets (N-MNIST [23], DVS-Gesture [24], CIFAR10-DVS [25]) support benchmarking.

Accuracy. The gap with conventional networks is narrowing but not yet closed:

  • Small-to-medium and event-based tasks: surrogate-gradient SNNs are now competitive with conventional networks, and the gap is nearly closed.
  • Large-scale (ImageNet): directly-trained SNNs reached about 75% top-1 accuracy in 2023 (Spikformer [26]) and roughly 80–81% by 2024 (Spikformer V2 [27]), against the 85–90%+ of leading vision transformers and convolutional networks, narrowing from wide to a few points but not yet closing.
  • Overall: the synthesis from Roy, Jaiswal & Panda [28] and the Eshraghian et al. tutorial [29]: the building blocks exist and the energy case is real on the right substrate, but no general-purpose, clearly-superior spiking system at scale has arrived yet.
  • The frontier: closing the accuracy gap while preserving sparsity, and developing learning rules that are both effective and hardware-local.

People and institutions

Foundations and theory. Wolfgang Maass (TU Graz) framed spiking networks as the third generation and established much of their computational theory. Eugene Izhikevich (then UCSD/NSI) gave the field its most-used efficient neuron model. Wulfram Gerstner (EPFL) co-authored the standard textbook Spiking Neuron Models. Terrence Sejnowski (Salk Institute) and Sander Bohte (CWI) contributed early coding and learning work.

Training methodology. Emre Neftci (now Forschungszentrum Jülich / RWTH Aachen) and Friedemann Zenke (Friedrich Miescher Institute, Basel) are central figures in surrogate-gradient learning. Timothée Masquelier (CNRS, Toulouse) works on STDP and temporal coding. Kaushik Roy (Purdue) leads spike-based deep learning and its hardware co-design. Jason Eshraghian (UC Santa Cruz) authored the widely-used snnTorch tutorial-paper and library.

Neuromorphic hardware. Carver Mead (Caltech) coined “neuromorphic” in the 1980s [30]. Giacomo Indiveri (Institute of Neuroinformatics, ETH Zurich / University of Zurich) is a leading mixed-signal neuromorphic engineer. Steve Furber (University of Manchester) built SpiNNaker [31]. The late Karlheinz Meier (Heidelberg) drove BrainScaleS. Dharmendra Modha led IBM TrueNorth [32] (and later NorthPole [20]). Mike Davies leads Intel’s Loihi [33] program. These efforts were heavily catalyzed by the EU Human Brain Project (2013–2023, now continued as the EBRAINS research infrastructure) and the US DARPA SyNAPSE program (2008–2014).

Today. The field’s center of gravity is shifting from big-science programs to a commercial wave: BrainChip (Akida), SynSense, and Innatera now ship neuromorphic silicon aimed at low-power edge sensing, while the academic side stays active through Intel’s Neuromorphic Research Community and continued SpiNNaker 2 work at Manchester and TU Dresden.

item.title: How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Artificial Analysis is an independent benchmarking outfit that ranks language models, and it publishes the full methodology behind its main metric, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. The page documents every evaluation in the index, how each is weighted and scored, and the exact testing parameters, down to sampling temperature and retry handling.

How the index works

The Intelligence Index (currently version 4.1) is a single 0–100 score built as a weighted average of nine evaluations across four categories. It is a text-only, English-language suite, and Artificial Analysis estimates a 95% confidence interval of under ±1% on the overall score. The nine weights sum to 100%, and the further benchmarks Artificial Analysis runs (multilingual, visual, mathematical, and several legacy evaluations) are reported separately and not counted in the index.

  • Four stated principles: every model is run under identical conditions (standardized); answer extraction is built to avoid penalizing valid output variations (unbiased); prompts give instructions without worked examples (zero-shot); and the full method, prompts, and limitations are published (transparent).

  • The nine evaluations and their weights, grouped by category:

    • Agents (34%): GDPval-AA v2 (20%), agentic completion of economically valuable tasks across 44 US occupations, with file outputs ranked into an Elo; and τ³-Banking (14%), a fintech customer-support agent built on Sierra’s τ-Knowledge framework that must combine knowledge retrieval with multi-step account changes.
    • Coding (24%): Terminal-Bench v2.1 (16%), 89 terminal tasks spanning software engineering, system administration, data processing, model training, and security, run through an agent in a sandbox; and SciCode (8%), Python scientific-computing problems scored by unit tests.
    • Scientific Reasoning (24%): Humanity’s Last Exam (12%), 2,158 open-answer frontier academic questions; GPQA Diamond (6%), 198 graduate-level Google-proof science questions; and CritPt (6%), 70 unpublished research-level physics problems.
    • General (18%): AA-Omniscience (12%), 6,000 questions over 42 topics scored by an index that rewards correct answers, penalizes hallucinations, and leaves abstentions neutral; and AA-LCR (6%), long-context reasoning over roughly 100,000-token document sets.

  • Testing parameters: temperature is 0 for non-reasoning models and 0.6 for reasoning models unless a lab recommends otherwise. Non-reasoning models get 16,384 output tokens, while reasoning models get their full disclosed budget. Failed API calls retry up to 30 times, and questions that never succeed are reviewed by hand and dropped.

  • Scoring and contamination handling: most evaluations use pass@1 averaged over one to five repeats, while GDPval-AA v2 uses an Elo from a three-judge panel, fit with a Bradley-Terry model and anchored to human experts at 1000. Artificial Analysis keeps internal copies of every dataset, and reports cost from provider-side token counts while standardizing performance on a client-side tokenizer.

Current results

As of June 2026, the Intelligence Index (v4.1) is led by Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.5, with a long tail of frontier models close behind.

The single score resolves into different profiles underneath, and Artificial Analysis also publishes category sub-indices. The Agentic Index averages the two agent benchmarks, GDPval-AA v2 and τ³-Banking:

The Coding Index averages Terminal-Bench v2.1 and SciCode, and the ranking shifts from the overall order, with GPT-5.5 moving up to second behind Claude Fable 5:

My Notes

  • Closed models lead all three indices: Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.5, all proprietary, take the top three on the overall index and on the agentic and coding sub-indices alike. The strongest open-weight model, GLM-5.2 from Zhipu, reaches fourth on the overall Intelligence Index, about nine points behind the leader. The open weights fall a clearer step behind on the agentic and coding charts, so the gap that has nearly closed on the broad knowledge-and-reasoning mix is still wide on the longer-horizon agentic and coding work.

    All four are reasoning models. Beyond that, disclosure differs sharply:

    • Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic): proprietary weights, no published parameter count or architecture.
    • Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic): proprietary weights, no published parameter count or architecture.
    • GPT-5.5 (OpenAI): proprietary weights, no published parameter count or architecture.
    • GLM-5.2 (Zhipu): open weights, 753B total parameters, a sparse mixture of experts (256 routed experts plus one shared, 8 active per token, 78 layers).

  • The method has limitations:

    • The weighting is an editorial choice: the index is a weighted average, and the weights reflect a judgment about what matters rather than a measurement. Agents are weighted most heavily, with GDPval-AA v2 alone a fifth of the score, so anyone comparing models on the one number inherits that bet. Ethayarajh and Jurafsky argued years ago that a leaderboard should let each reader set their own weights instead of shipping one ranking for everyone.
    • Several components are public benchmarks: Humanity’s Last Exam, GPQA Diamond, SciCode, and Terminal-Bench are all openly available, so training-data contamination is a live risk. The defenses are internal copies of every dataset and the evaluations Artificial Analysis built itself, a weaker defense than the post-cutoff, unpublished questions the Leipzig math benchmark used to stay out of the training data.
    • An LLM panel grades the heaviest evaluation: GDPval-AA v2, the largest single component, scores agentic deliverables by an Elo from a panel of three frontier model judges, anchored to human experts at 1000. The panel reduces the bias any single judge would bring, but the score still measures what frontier models agree is good work, which can differ from what a human expert would rank first.
    • The compared models are black boxes: the closed leaders disclose neither parameter count nor architecture, so the index ranks delivered capability without controlling for model size, design, or training compute. Only the open-weight entrants publish those details, and cost per task, which Artificial Analysis reports separately, is the nearest proxy for what a score costs to reach.

Related Posts

  • Utility Is in the Eye of the User: the case that benchmark utility is user-specific and leaderboards should let readers set their own weights, a direct counterpoint to collapsing nine evaluations into one fixed-weight index.
  • Benchmarks in Leipzig: a benchmark built from fresh, post-cutoff, unpublished questions to resist contamination, the stronger defense the public components of this index lack.
  • Mapping Global Dynamics of Benchmark Creation and Saturation in AI: the create-then-saturate cycle that explains why an index has to keep swapping in harder evaluations to stay informative.
  • Anthropic Economic Index: another attempt to measure model capability on economically valuable work, and a reminder that a metric designed not to saturate (time horizon) is a different bet than a fixed-question score.

item.title: A Juneteenth Run to Lincoln Park
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:

To honor this Juneteenth I decided to run from the office to Lincoln Park in West Seattle: distance 13.8mi moving time 2:27:38 pace 10’42”/mi.

It was also a day for the World Cup: US vs Australia, both playing the second game. Seattle was buzzing with people from all over the world: parade, music, just a high level of energy everywhere!

(the choppers flying formation back and forth a few times, probably for the game)

Weather was pretty warm: felt like 75F with 2.2mph wind. Luckily the sun was not as menacing as expected. Alki beach was surprisingly calm – people probably all flooded downtown for the game!

After an 8mi run I stopped at Alki beach park to have my favorite clam chowder cup soup for a light lunch, then continued on.

There were swimming meets at Colman Pool. I also finally found the troll: her name is Bruun Idun – a young teenage troll who plays her flute to the orca whales!

On the bus back, the riders broke into cheers when someone announced that the US had just won the game 2–0! ⚽️

Here’s a video recap of today’s run from Seattle to Lincoln Park to honor Juneteenth.

item.title: The ACUTE Protocol: Operationalizing Language Model Activations for Better Calibration, Utility, and Trust
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In The ACUTE Protocol: Operationalizing Language Model Activations for Better Calibration, Utility, and Trust [1] (ICML 2026), Nishant Subramani, Palash Goyal, Yiwen Song, Mani Malek, Yuan Xue, Tomas Pfister, and Hamid Palangi (CMU, Google, Scale AI) train lightweight classifiers on a model’s own hidden states to decide when to trust its output, and propose a utility metric, EURO, that scores confidence estimates on whether they help a downstream decision rather than on calibration alone.

As language models improve and become increasingly deployed to solve a variety of tasks, trustworthiness becomes essential. Calibration is a good proxy for trust: well-calibrated confidence estimates help inform the risk versus reward tradeoff when trusting a specific model output. Unfortunately, even as models improve, they remain poorly calibrated, often biasing towards overconfidence. Additionally, calibration can be gamed: a policy that always predicts the base rate is perfectly calibrated, but completely uninformative. To resolve this, we develop a new metric, expected utility renormalized by the oracle (EURO), that balances calibration and informativeness. We also propose a general-purpose activation-based confidence, utility, and trust estimation protocol (ACUTE) to appropriately adjudicate uncertainty. The ACUTE protocol provides flexible, sample-efficient, and compute-efficient confidence estimators for 3 tasks including multiple choice question answering, tool-calling, and scientific document summarization across 6 models from 4 model families. ACUTE outperforms strong baselines on EURO, while maintaining low calibration error. Taken together, our work shows that equipping LLMs with the ACUTE protocol can improve calibration, utility, and trustworthiness in numerous settings.

Methods

The paper has two parts: a metric EURO and a confidence estimator ACUTE.

EURO (expected utility renormalized by the oracle) answers a complaint about calibration scores. The expected calibration error (ECE) and its smoothed variant (smECE) measure whether stated confidences match observed accuracy, but a model that reports the base rate on every example is perfectly calibrated and useless. EURO instead frames confidence as a trust-or-abstain decision and scores the utility of acting on it, in four steps:

  • Assign rewards to the four outcomes: the trust-or-abstain decision has four cases, each with a task-set reward. Trusting a correct answer earns , abstaining on a wrong one earns , trusting a wrong one earns , and abstaining on a correct one earns , with correct calls rewarded () and mistakes penalized ().
  • Reduce them to one knob.
    • Net utilities: is the gain from correctly trusting a correct answer instead of abstaining, and the gain from correctly abstaining on a wrong answer instead of trusting. The subtracted terms are penalties (), so each difference is the full swing between the two outcomes.
    • Normalize: rescale the pair to sum to one, and .
    • The threshold falls out: the minimum-Bayes-risk threshold works out to exactly , so the estimator trusts when its confidence exceeds . A plain classifier (reward 1 for a correct call, 0 for a mistake) gives .
    • Penalties steer it: making a wrong trust expensive () raises toward 1, so the estimator demands more confidence before trusting, while making a wrong abstention expensive () grows and lowers toward 0, so it trusts more readily.
  • Renormalize to a fixed scale: score the estimator’s utility at a given against a perfect oracle (1) and a worst-case anti-oracle (0), so the number is comparable across tasks.
  • Sweep risk levels: the four rewards are application-specific, so rather than fix them per task the experiments leave them unset and sweep across its whole range , which is enough because collapses the reward structure into that one number. The area under the resulting curve, auc-euro, is the headline number, reported both over the full range and over three bins: low , medium , and high , identically across MMLU, APIGen, and SCITLDR.

Figure 1 shows why this matters: ECE and smECE rank the two worst estimators (a base-rate predictor and a noisy base-rate predictor) above a probabilistic oracle, while auc-euro orders all four correctly.

ACUTE (activation-based confidence, utility, and trust estimation) is the estimator. For each output it reads the model’s internal activations and trains a random forest to predict whether the output is correct. The features aren’t concatenated into one model: each of three feature families trains its own estimator, and the paper reports six configurations in total:

  • Mean-pooled activations: the hidden states at a layer, averaged over tokens. Trained per layer, this yields three configurations, the best estimator from the early, middle, and late third of layers (acute early/mid/late act).
  • Layer-wise cosine similarities with the final layer: a low-dimensional summary of how each layer’s activation aligns with the last, one configuration (acute cosine).
  • PCA-transformed activations: a layer’s activations reduced to their top 10 or 20 principal components, two configurations (acute pca10, acute pca20).

Random forests are the classifier throughout because they slightly outperformed logistic regression and support vector machines in early experiments, and because a well-trained forest needs no post-hoc recalibration. A single decision tree reads its probability off leaf purity and pushes toward 0 or 1, the reason tree estimators have traditionally needed post-hoc scaling such as Platt scaling [2] [3]. A forest instead reports the vote fraction across many decorrelated trees, a smoother estimate that is already close to calibrated when the forest is well-trained [4].

Results

The protocol is evaluated on six models from four families (gemma-3-4b-it, gemma-3-12b-it, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-14B, phi-4, and SmolLM3-3B) across three deliberately distinct tasks: MMLU multiple-choice question answering [5] (5-shot, scored over its 57 subtasks), APIGen tool-calling [6] (zero-shot, approximate exact match), and SCITLDR scientific-abstract summarization [7] (zero-shot, ROUGE-L). The two generation tasks force the estimator to work from multi-token output, not a single classification logit. ACUTE’s six configurations are compared against raw confidences and two strong, cheap baselines, a histogram regression estimator (HRE) and Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression (NWKR), with calibration measured by smECE (lower is better) and utility by auc-euro (higher is better) at low, medium, and high risk.

The headline numbers (Table 1, averaged across models) decompose by task:

  • Tool-calling shows the largest gain. On APIGen, acute pca20 reaches 0.88 auc-euro versus 0.78 for both HRE and NWKR, roughly 0.10 ahead of the strong baselines and 0.35 ahead of raw confidences (0.53).
  • Multiple-choice shows a modest gain. On MMLU, acute late act reaches 0.83 versus 0.79 for NWKR, with the edge concentrated at high risk (0.80 versus 0.74).
  • Summarization shows essentially none. On SCITLDR, every method including the histogram baseline scores 0.77–0.78, and ACUTE matches the baselines without beating them.
  • Calibration holds throughout. smECE stays low (around 0.07–0.09), comparable to the calibration baselines, so the utility gains do not come at the cost of miscalibration.

Figure 4 shows where that high-risk edge on MMLU comes from. The y-axis is EURO, the oracle-renormalized expected utility where 1.0 matches a perfect oracle and higher is better. The x-axis is the risk level , the normalized abstention utility defined above (equivalently the trust threshold ), running from low-risk settings on the left to high-risk on the right, where wrongly trusting a bad answer is costliest. Each line is one estimator, one of the three baselines or ACUTE’s six configurations, averaged over the 57 MMLU subtasks. At low risk, where abstaining is cheap, every estimator including the baselines performs about the same and the curves overlap. As the risk level rises the ACUTE estimators pull away from raw confidences, HRE, and NWKR, which is why ACUTE’s MMLU advantage is modest in the pooled score but pronounced at high risk.

The analysis sections add three supporting results:

  • Sample-efficient. ACUTE reaches its accuracy with small training sets.
  • Middle and late layers win. Those depths give the strongest mean-pooled signal.
  • Generalizes to a mixture-of-experts model. On Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (Table 2), an MoE with 30B total but only ~3B active parameters, acute pca20 and acute late act reach roughly 0.87 auc-euro on APIGen against about 0.82 for the calibration baselines, with the SCITLDR result flat again. The active footprint is on par with the smallest dense models tested, so this checks the MoE architecture rather than a larger compute budget.

My Notes

  • What EURO adds beyond proper scores. EURO is motivated by the fact that ECE rewards a base-rate predictor, the failure I worked through in a primer on calibration metrics, where a constant-0.5 model scores a perfect zero while saying nothing. But the Brier score and log loss already can’t be gamed that way, so EURO’s real addition is the risk-level framing (proper scores already resist gaming): it scores confidence by the utility of trusting or abstaining and sweeps that utility across risk levels. The paper’s Appendix B agrees: minimizing the Brier score gives a Bayes-optimal predictor, but Brier still ignores the task’s risk level, the same blind spot as ECE.
  • It needs access to the model’s internals. ACUTE reads activations, so only whoever holds the weights can run it, which the paper accepts as fine for model developers. That makes it a first-party tool, unlike verbalized confidence (Just Ask for Calibration) or logit-based self-knowledge (Kadavath et al.), which a caller can use through an API. It is closest to reading confidence off the residual stream (metacognitive monitoring and control through activations), but trains an external probe instead of asking the model to report on itself.
  • The gain depends on the scoring metric. ACUTE helps a lot on tool-calling, a little on multiple choice, and not at all on summarization. Tool-calling is judged by near-exact match, close to a yes/no, while a ROUGE-L summary score is fuzzy, and there even the histogram baseline is near the ceiling. The activation signal for whether an answer is right seems strongest when “right” is close to binary, which suggests ACUTE will help most on verifiable tasks and least on open-ended generation.

References

item.title: Policy on the AI Exponential
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, argues that AI capability is racing ahead of the institutions meant to govern it, and uses a new essay to lay out what governments should do across five policy areas before the gap widens. The essay opens with Treebeard, the ponderous tree who takes a full day to say hello while his forest is cut down.

The essay covers five policy areas:

  • Regulation and public safety: model frontier-AI oversight on agencies like the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), with mandatory pre-deployment testing and the power to block models judged unsafe.
  • Macroeconomics and tax policy: treat enduring job displacement as a danger to minimize, not a future to bring about, through better measurement, pro-employment incentives, and eventually long-term income support such as universal basic income.
  • Accelerating AI’s positive impact: reform slow approval pipelines (the 7-8 year drug timeline at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA)) so AI-driven science is not jammed, starting with standards for accepting AI simulation in place of some trials.
  • The state and civil liberties: accountability rules and a domestic ban for autonomous weapons, closing the data-broker surveillance loophole, and a public right to AI at least as capable as the government’s during adverse action.
  • Securing leadership by democracies: a coalition of democracies that shares the chip supply chain internally and denies it to adversaries, coordinates risk regulation, and provides mutual defense.

Along with the essay, Anthropic released a legislative proposal on frontier-model testing and a policy framework for job displacement, both with promised financial backing. The essay summarizes the testing proposal in five elements, with the full version published as Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework:

  • Mandatory third-party testing for models above a compute threshold, in four risk areas: cybersecurity, biological weapons, loss of control, and automated R&D.
  • Power to block or deter deployment when a third-party assessment finds unacceptable risk, scoped to those four risks and with safeguards against political favoritism.
  • A choice of evaluator: a government agency like the FAA, or private organizations authorized and inspected by the government (a “regulatory markets” approach).
  • Security standards to protect model weights, with regular red teaming, penetration testing, and cooperation with government against major threat actors.
  • Prompt reporting of safety incidents in the four critical areas.

The US Suspends Fable 5 and Mythos 5

Shortly after the essay, its argument about blocking deployments got a real-world test. On June 12, 2026, the US government issued an export-control directive, citing national security, ordering Anthropic to suspend all access to its newest models, Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5, for any foreign national inside or outside the country, including the company’s own foreign-national employees. To comply, Anthropic disabled both models for every customer. Its other models were not affected.

The government’s stated concern was a technique for jailbreaking Fable 5. Anthropic says it reviewed the demonstration and found only a few minor, previously known vulnerabilities that other public models, including OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, can find without any bypass. It is complying with the order but disagrees that a narrow jailbreak should justify recalling a model already deployed to hundreds of millions of people, and argues that the same standard applied across the industry would halt frontier deployment altogether.

The essay had argued that the government should be able to block unsafe deployments, but only through a statutory process that is “transparent, fair, clear, and grounded in technical facts.” Anthropic’s statement on the directive says the action “does not adhere to those principles.”

Related Posts

  • The Anthropic Institute’s Research Agenda: Anthropic’s own four-pillar agenda on economic diffusion, threats, and AI-driven R&D, the institutional counterpart to this policy essay.
  • Anthropic Economic Index: the measurement effort Amodei cites as the kind of labor-market data governments should expand to track displacement.
  • Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy: the counterweight on job displacement, arguing the replace-not-augment direction is a policy choice rather than an intrinsic property.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: a concrete version of the fast-displacement scenario the macroeconomics section worries about.
  • OpenAI’s Five Principles for AGI: a peer lab’s governance statement, useful next to Anthropic’s more prescriptive policy asks.

item.title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes [1] (arXiv preprint, May 2026), Matt Y. Cheung, Ashok Veeraraghavan, Hanjie Chen, and Guha Balakrishnan (Rice University) introduce CROP, a calibration layer that returns the longest leading slice of a reasoning trace whose steps provably contain no annotated error, given any step-level risk signal.

Language model reasoning traces are rarely all-or-nothing; they frequently contain valid intermediate steps before a critical error occurs. Existing uncertainty quantification methods typically certify final answers or entire responses, failing to provide statistical guarantees for the proportion of a sequential trace that can be safely retained. To address this, we introduce CROP (Conformal Reasoning Output Prefixes), a verifier-agnostic calibration procedure for clean-prefix certification. Given any step-level risk proxy, CROP selects a calibrated threshold and returns the longest contiguous prefix whose step risk proxies remain below it, routing the uncertified suffix for downstream review or repair. Assuming exchangeability, CROP rigorously controls the marginal probability that the returned prefix contains an annotated error. Across six process-labeled reasoning datasets, we demonstrate that standard step-level metrics such as AUROC do not fully capture prefix utility, suggesting verifiers should instead be evaluated by certified prefix length. Furthermore, CROP balances over- and under-withholding, improving downstream repair accuracy by preserving valid intermediate reasoning while discarding misleading suffixes. Ultimately, this work positions prefix certification as a rigorous, practical bridge between process supervision, abstention, and repair.

Methods

CROP operates downstream of a completed reasoning trace and asks a narrower question than most uncertainty quantification (UQ) work. Not “is the final answer right?” but “how much of this trace can I keep before the first error?” A reasoning instance is a question plus its trace of steps, each step labeled with a binary error flag in the data. CROP turns step-level risk scores into a single calibrated cut-off, then keeps everything up to that cut-off. The pieces:

  • Step-level risk proxy: a fixed function that scores each step, with larger values meaning higher estimated error risk. The proxy can be a process reward model (PRM), a model trained to judge whether each reasoning step is correct (the kind of step scorer the literature calls a verifier), or a plainer signal such as a likelihood statistic, a hidden-state feature, or a hand-built heuristic. CROP is verifier-agnostic: it consumes whatever the proxy outputs, which need not be calibrated or even accurate, only fixed before calibration.
  • Retained prefix: at a threshold , CROP keeps the longest leading run of steps whose risk all stays at or below , a prefix of length . The uncertified suffix after the first threshold crossing is split off for downstream review or repair.
  • Monotone contamination loss: for an instance , the loss flags the failure event “the kept prefix contains an annotated error.” Because raising can only lengthen the prefix, and once a bad step enters it never leaves, this binary loss is monotone in . Monotonicity is the condition conformal risk control (CRC) [2] requires, so CROP applies it directly.
  • Calibration rule: on held-out labeled instances and a target risk , CROP picks the largest threshold whose corrected empirical contamination rate (the mean loss over those instances, with the a finite-sample correction) stays at or below . A larger means longer prefixes, so this is the longest prefix subject to the risk budget. If no threshold qualifies, it falls back to the empty prefix.

The guarantee that follows, the paper’s Proposition 1, Clean-Prefix Risk Control, is finite-sample and marginal: under exchangeability of the calibration and test instances, the returned prefix contains an annotated error with probability at most . Writing for the calibrated threshold and for a fresh instance, that is . The reason is the standard split-conformal count: the calibration rule sets so that at most of the calibration instances come out contaminated, and a fresh instance, being exchangeable with those , is equally likely to fall at any rank among the , so its chance of landing in the contaminated group is at most . The exchangeable unit is the whole instance, not the step, so steps inside a trace may depend on each other arbitrarily.

The cover figure shows what CROP produces on two worked traces: a green certified prefix, a red uncertified suffix, and a blue repair pass on the suffix. The Arithmetic example clears its prefix at a strict threshold (). The GSM8K example, where the proxy is noisier, certifies far less () and cuts after the second step. Each here is its dataset’s single calibrated threshold, fixed once on that dataset’s calibration split and applied to every instance, so the two values differ because they come from two separate calibrations, not because is tuned per problem. What changes from trace to trace is only where that fixed threshold falls.

Results

The authors evaluate CROP across six process-supervision datasets: Arithmetic and GSM8K (Llama-generated chain-of-thought traces with dense first-error labels, from the circuit-based reasoning verification (CRV) dataset [7]), plus ProcessBench [8], Math-Shepherd [9], PRMBench [10], and PRM800K [3]. The main benchmark is 2,819 traces over Arithmetic and GSM8K (19,311 steps, 1,006 annotated errors).

They compare five step-level risk proxies on a 60/20/20 train/calibration/test split:

  • Random: random step scores, the floor baseline.
  • Token/format: a logistic regression over cheap text features (step length, position, punctuation).
  • Trace features: a logistic regression over those text features plus Llama-3.1-8B likelihood and hidden-state summaries.
  • Direct PRM: a frozen Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B, scored directly as one minus its step-correctness probability.
  • Trace features + PRM: a joint logistic regression over the trace features and the PRM score.

The target risk is fixed at , and downstream repair is measured by feeding the certified prefix to four separate repair models (Gemma 4, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, Llama3.1-8B) and parsing the final answer.

CROP’s repair is compared against three baseline interfaces:

  • Question-only: the repair model sees only the original question, with the trace discarded entirely.
  • Full-trace: the repair model sees the complete trace, warned that it may contain mistakes.
  • Conformal whole-trace abstention: an all-or-nothing conformal decision that either accepts the entire trace or backs off to the bare question, with no partial prefix.

At a fixed risk target, the more of each trace CROP can certify, the better, since the certified prefix is valid reasoning kept for downstream use rather than discarded. Figure 2 plots this retained-prefix fraction as the risk target is relaxed.

The findings:

  • AUROC does not predict prefix utility. Step-level AUROC (the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) measures how well a proxy ranks erroneous steps above correct ones, the usual yardstick for choosing among proxies. Here it is the wrong one: Figure 3’s red segments mark inversions where the higher-AUROC of two proxies certifies the shorter prefix, and the appendix proves two proxies can share identical AUROC yet certify different prefix lengths under the same calibration. The paper recommends selecting proxies by certified prefix length instead.
  • PRM signals dominate, and not as an artifact. PRM-backed proxies retained the longest prefixes at fixed risk across datasets (for example 97.5% retained on Arithmetic and 81.7% on GSM8K at , versus 77.5% and 39.8% for token/format). After balancing trace length, formatting, and answer-format cues, PRM still kept ~27 percentage points more prefix than the token/format baseline, so the gain is not explained by exploitable formatting regularities.
  • CROP’s cut is closer to the oracle clean boundary. Against the annotated first-error position, CROP’s boundary deviation was 1.1% on Arithmetic and 9.9% on GSM8K, beating whole-trace abstention (4.6% and 14.1%) by avoiding both over-withholding of clean steps and unsafe overshoot past the first error.
  • Repair gains are real but model-dependent. CROP beat the best deployable non-CROP input in five of eight repair settings, with the largest lift on Arithmetic for DeepSeek (+5.5 points) and Gemma (+5.3). Llama posted negative deltas in both domains, which the authors trace to same-family answer repetition: the Arithmetic and GSM8K traces were originally generated by Llama, so the Llama repair model is unusually prone to copying the trace’s own wrong answer.

Figure 3 ties the first two findings together: PRM proxies retain the most prefix, but the red segments show that moving to a higher-AUROC proxy sometimes costs retained prefix.

Beyond accuracy, CROP changes what the downstream workflow sees. Whole-trace abstention is all-or-nothing: it accepts a full trace or falls back to the bare question. CROP instead returns a partial prefix, salvaging the clean opening of traces that abstention would reject outright.

Table 3 shows the tradeoff: with the PRM proxies, CROP keeps more total step mass (92.0% and 95.1%) than whole-trace abstention at a matched empirical risk, even while accepting fewer whole traces.

My Notes

  • CROP extends the conformal-for-LLMs line to a new object. Conformal Language Modeling [4] certifies a set of candidate generations, and Conformal Thinking [5] calibrates stop/continue thresholds for a compute budget. CROP applies the same conformal risk control [2] machinery to a third object, a contiguous reasoning prefix.
  • The coverage guarantee holds in aggregate, not per question. Like all conformal prediction [6], CROP controls the contamination probability averaged over the calibration distribution, so a particular question from a topic rare in that set can still contaminate well above .
  • Rewarding global ranking does not necessarily yield the longest prefixes at a fixed risk. The process-reward-model literature CROP builds on, from PRM800K and Let’s Verify Step by Step [3] onward, ranks proxies by pooled step accuracy and best-of- selection, both global-ranking objectives. Prefix certification instead rewards keeping the opening clean, so a PRM that tops those leaderboards need not certify the longest prefix at the same risk. A deployment that cares about prefix length should re-rank its proxies by certified prefix length directly.

  2. Angelopoulos, A. N., Bates, S., Fisch, A., Lei, L., and Schuster, T. “Conformal Risk Control.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024). arXiv:2208.02814. https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02814

This Long Run Sunday I ran my 82nd HM on East Sammamish Lake Trail: distance 14mi, moving time 2:11:12, pace 9’22”/mi.

There’s a heat advisory and by the time I finished it felt like 80F. And no wind (0.2mph). I brought my usual 8oz eletrolyte and 2 gels and consumed them all.

(but I should feel lucky because much of the world is suffering from even higher temperature)

There was a trail closure at 3.9mi and I had to detour to road for .5mi and came back.

My swollen knees from the fall 2 days ago are mostly gone, and the wounds are “mostly” dried – that’s why I decided to give it a go. Turned out it went pretty well: my avg/max HR was 139/155bpm (sped up a bit in the last mile), and VO2max is now 51.2.

We’ll see how I feel tomorrow morning. 😛
